question: A 68-year-old man with known multiple myeloma and chronic kidney disease has diffuse bone pain. A technetium 99m bone scan reports several photopenic areas in the ribs and skull, while skeletal survey radiographs show punched out lesions in the same regions. What best explains the cold areas on the scan?

options.A: Poor renal clearance of radiotracer, producing diffuse blurring that mimics isolated cold defects
options.B: Lytic marrow replacement with little osteoblastic repair, so scant radiotracer is taken up
options.C: Technical error from a delayed imaging time, since cold lesions appear only on very late images
options.D: Hypervascular bone lesions with brisk blood flow that wash tracer out before uptake can occur

explanation: The correct answer is B (Lytic marrow replacement with little osteoblastic repair, so scant radiotracer is taken up): Technetium methylene diphosphonate uptake depends on osteoblastic activity and blood flow, and myeloma lesions are mainly lytic with little new bone formation. That is why myeloma is often missed or shown as cold areas on a bone scan, and why a skeletal survey or MRI is preferred. Poor renal clearance raises soft tissue background diffusely rather than creating discrete photopenia. Delayed timing does not turn lesions cold.

question: A 44-year-old accountant with chronic low back pain sits ten hours daily. He says he bought walking shoes, joined a gym that he will start next Monday, and plans to walk after work three evenings weekly. He has not yet begun any exercise. Using the transtheoretical model, which intervention best matches his current stage of change?

options.A: Review strategies to prevent relapse and handle high risk situations such as business travel
options.B: Help him write a specific walking schedule with a start date and plans for expected obstacles
options.C: Give education on the health risks of sedentary work to raise his awareness of the problem
options.D: Explore his ambivalence about whether the benefits of exercise outweigh the time and effort

explanation: The correct answer is B (Help him write a specific walking schedule with a start date and plans for expected obstacles): In the preparation stage the patient intends to act soon and has taken small steps, so the best help is a concrete, time bound action plan with barriers anticipated. Risk education suits precontemplation, when the patient does not yet see a problem. Ambivalence exploration suits contemplation, which he has passed. Relapse prevention belongs to maintenance, after the behavior has been sustained for months.

question: A 45 year old woman has right upper abdominal pain after fatty meals and a deep ache at the tip of her right shoulder blade. Her spine moves freely and is not tender. Which explanation accounts for the shoulder blade pain and shows it is not spinal?

options.A: Gallbladder swelling presses on the T4 nerve root as it exits the middle thoracic spine
options.B: Inflammation irritates the sympathetic chain, sending pain to the T10 and T11 dermatomes
options.C: Diaphragm irritation travels in the phrenic nerve, which shares C3 to C5 segments with the shoulder
options.D: The vagus nerve carries gallbladder pain signals to C1 and C2 segments at the skull base

explanation: The correct answer is C (Diaphragm irritation travels in the phrenic nerve, which shares C3 to C5 segments with the shoulder): The gallbladder lies against the diaphragm, and peritoneal irritation travels in the phrenic nerve, which arises from C3, C4 and C5. The brain reads that input as coming from the same segments that supply the right shoulder and scapula. Because the cause is visceral, spinal motion is normal and nontender. The other options name incorrect nerves or levels.

question: A 58-year-old man has no patellar reflex on the right, with quadriceps strength 2 out of 5 and visible thigh fasciculations. Light touch and pinprick over the anterior thigh and medial leg are normal. Using the reflex arc components in order, which part of the arc has failed?

options.A: Effector quadriceps muscle fiber itself, as occurs in a primary myopathy with preserved nerve supply
options.B: Efferent alpha motor neuron to the quadriceps, with the sensory limb and spinal integration spared
options.C: Afferent Ia neuron from the muscle spindle, since sensation travels along the same axons
options.D: Integration center in the L2 to L4 spinal cord, where the single synapse lies

explanation: The correct answer is B (Efferent alpha motor neuron to the quadriceps, with the sensory limb and spinal integration spared): Normal sensation argues against failure of the afferent limb, and fasciculations with weakness indicate a lower motor neuron problem. The efferent alpha motor neuron to the quadriceps is the failed component. A myopathy would not typically produce fasciculations. A cord synapse lesion would usually affect other tracts and levels as well.

question: A 45-year-old woman treated with radioactive iodine for Graves disease three years ago has swollen hands and rounded fingertips. She is a nonsmoker and her chest film is normal. Pain is mild and symmetric. An anteroposterior hand radiograph is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis and the clinical sign that accompanies it?

options.A: Hyperparathyroidism, with subperiosteal resorption along the radial side of the middle phalanges
options.B: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy from lung cancer, which produces linear periostitis of long bones with clubbing
options.C: Psoriatic arthritis, with fluffy periostitis at joints and pencil-in-cup deformities of the distal joints
options.D: Thyroid acropachy, a rare Graves disease complication with clubbing and spiculated periosteal bone in the hands

explanation: The correct answer is D (Thyroid acropachy, a rare Graves disease complication with clubbing and spiculated periosteal bone in the hands): Thyroid acropachy follows treated Graves disease and combines soft tissue swelling, clubbing, and solid or spiculated periosteal new bone in the metacarpals and phalanges. The normal chest film and nonsmoking history argue against hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, and it usually involves long bones rather than the hand alone. Hyperparathyroidism removes bone surface instead of adding periosteum, and psoriatic arthritis has joint erosions that are absent here.

question: A plastic surgeon plans an elective incision on the forearm of a 34-year-old man and orients the cut parallel to the natural tension lines of the skin rather than across them. When asked, she explains the anatomical reasoning to the patient. What is the basis for orienting the incision this way?

options.A: Superficial veins run along these lines, so parallel cuts avoid major bleeding during wound closure
options.B: Dermal collagen fibers run in one direction, so parallel cuts gap less and scar more narrowly
options.C: Dermatomes run along these lines, so parallel cuts spare sensory branches and preserve skin sensation
options.D: Fascial attachments align with these lines, so parallel cuts avoid separating skin from deep fascia

explanation: The correct answer is B (Dermal collagen fibers run in one direction, so parallel cuts gap less and scar more narrowly): Langer lines reflect the dominant orientation of dermal collagen fibers. An incision parallel to them is under less lateral tension, so the edges stay together and the scar is thinner. Dermatomes describe segmental sensory supply and do not define tension lines. Venous patterns and fascial attachments do not determine the lines either.

question: A 63-year-old man reports eight months of aching on the right side, a limp each morning, and discomfort after long standing. He denies back pain, and his lumbar motion is normal on examination. The chiropractor must separate a hip joint source from referred lumbar pain. Which two history features in the chart best favor the hip joint? (Select 2)

options.A: Pain is felt in the groin and anterior thigh rather than the buttock or lower back
options.B: Stiffness lasts more than two hours and affects hands and wrists too
options.C: Pain is relieved by lumbar flexion and worsened by walking downhill
options.D: Pain travels below the knee in a dermatomal pattern with tingling
options.E: Stiffness after rising lasts about 20 minutes and eases with walking

explanation: The correct answers are A and E: Hip joint disease refers pain to the groin and anterior thigh, whereas lumbar sources usually refer to the buttock and posterior thigh. Morning stiffness under 30 minutes that improves with use is typical of osteoarthritis. Relief with flexion and worse downhill walking suggests stenosis, long stiffness with multiple joints suggests inflammatory disease, and dermatomal radiation suggests a root lesion. None of those appear in this history.

Patient: M, 63 y, 70 in, 218 lb
Vitals: Pulse 72, resp 16, BP 136/84 mmHg, temp 98.4 F
Chief complaint and history: Eight months of right groin and anterior thigh ache. He limps and feels stiff for about 20 minutes on rising, easing as he walks, and the ache returns after long standing. Pain 5/10 after yard work. No back pain, night pain, fever or weight loss. BMI 31. Takes acetaminophen occasionally.
Examination: Antalgic gait with shortened right stance phase. Mild right gluteal and quadriceps atrophy. Lumbar flexion and extension full and painless. Passive hip motion right: flexion 95, internal rotation 5, external rotation 30, abduction 30 degrees. Left: flexion 120, internal rotation 35, external rotation 45.
Orthopedic and neurological tests: FABER on the right reproduces groin pain and is limited. Hip scour is painful with crepitus. Straight leg raise and femoral nerve stretch negative bilaterally. Trendelenburg mildly positive right. Patellar and Achilles reflexes 2+. Lower limb strength 5/5, sensation intact.
Laboratory and imaging: ESR 12 mm/hr, CRP 0.4 mg/dL. AP pelvis: asymmetric superolateral narrowing of the right hip joint space, marginal osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis of the femoral head and acetabulum. Sacroiliac joints appear normal.

question: The examiner measures passive hip motion bilaterally in this 63-year-old man and tests him with several provocative maneuvers. Lumbar motion is full and painless, and straight leg raise is negative. Considering only positive findings recorded in the chart, which two most directly localize the problem to the hip joint rather than the lumbar spine or muscles? (Select 2)

options.A: Normal ESR and CRP values with no systemic symptoms
options.B: Passive internal rotation is limited to 5 degrees compared with 35 degrees on the left
options.C: Antalgic gait with a shortened stance phase on the right
options.D: Mild atrophy of the right gluteal and quadriceps muscles
options.E: FABER reproduces the groin pain and the right hip is limited in that position

explanation: The correct answers are B and E: Loss of hip internal rotation is the earliest and most reliable sign of hip joint disease, and a painful, restricted FABER stresses the joint and reproduces groin pain. Atrophy and an antalgic gait follow pain from many lower limb problems, so they do not localize to the hip. Normal inflammatory markers help exclude infection or inflammatory arthritis but do not point to a specific joint.

question: The pelvis radiograph of this 63-year-old man shows moderate narrowing of the right hip joint space with osteophytes. His pain is 5/10 after yard work, he has no rest pain, he carries extra weight and he limps. He is willing to follow a program. Which two actions fit his care at this stage? (Select 2)

options.A: Apply high-velocity long-axis thrust to the hip as the main treatment to restore joint space
options.B: Refer to orthopedics if night pain appears or function declines despite three months of care
options.C: Prescribe a cane held in the right hand to share load with the painful hip
options.D: Prescribe low-impact aerobic and hip strengthening exercise with weight reduction toward a lower BMI
options.E: Refer now for total hip arthroplasty because the radiograph shows joint space narrowing

explanation: The correct answers are B and D: Exercise and weight loss reduce joint load and pain in hip osteoarthritis, and a trial of about three months of conservative care is typical before surgical consideration. Rest pain, night pain or declining function despite care are indications for orthopedic referral. A cane belongs in the hand opposite the painful hip, so the right-hand cane fails. Radiographic narrowing alone does not justify surgery, and thrust manipulation cannot restore cartilage.

question: A 34-year-old office worker wakes with a painful, taut band in the right upper trapezius after a long night of laptop work. Motion is limited by pain, there was no trauma, and the neurologic exam is normal. Which soft tissue approach best addresses the tender nodule that refers pain toward the temple?

options.A: Rapid percussive tapotement over the muscle belly for several minutes to fatigue the fibers
options.B: Deep transverse friction applied briskly across the nodule for ten minutes to break up adhesions
options.C: Sustained pressure on the tender nodule, then gentle myofascial release along the fibers
options.D: Passive stretch of the muscle into full end range, held until the patient reports sharp pain

explanation: The correct answer is C (Sustained pressure on the tender nodule, then gentle myofascial release along the fibers): Trigger point pressure held at a tolerable level lets the taut band release, and myofascial release then lengthens the surrounding fascia without provoking more guarding. Deep friction suits chronic tendon problems, not an irritable acute spasm. Stretching to sharp pain or using percussive tapotement stimulates the muscle and increases protective tone.

question: A 45-year-old woman has no hip pain but a waddling gait. When she stands on her right leg alone, her left pelvis drops below the level of the right. The examiner records a positive Trendelenburg sign. Which muscle weakness and nerve supply explain this finding?

options.A: Right gluteus maximus weakness, from the inferior gluteal nerve, mainly impairing hip extension when rising
options.B: Left gluteus medius weakness, because the pelvis falls on the side of the weak abductor
options.C: Right iliopsoas weakness, from the femoral nerve, mainly impairing hip flexion during stair climbing
options.D: Right gluteus medius weakness, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve from the L4 to S1 roots

explanation: The correct answer is D (Right gluteus medius weakness, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve from the L4 to S1 roots): During single-leg stance the gluteus medius on the stance leg holds the pelvis level, so a drop on the opposite side means the stance-side muscle is weak, here the right. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, L4 to S1. The gluteus maximus extends the hip and the iliopsoas flexes it, so neither produces this sign.

question: A 66-year-old retired mail carrier reports calf cramping after two blocks of walking that resolves within minutes of rest. His feet feel cool and his dorsalis pedis pulses are faint on both sides. You measure an ankle brachial index of 0.6 on the right. What does this value most likely indicate?

options.A: Medial arterial calcification producing a falsely low reading, so the result should be discarded and repeated
options.B: Chronic venous insufficiency from valve reflux, the usual cause of exertional calf cramping with cool feet
options.C: Normal arterial perfusion, because resting index values between 0.5 and 1.0 are expected in healthy adults
options.D: Moderate peripheral arterial disease with reduced limb perfusion, explaining his intermittent claudication from arterial narrowing

explanation: The correct answer is D (Moderate peripheral arterial disease with reduced limb perfusion, explaining his intermittent claudication from arterial narrowing): An ankle brachial index is ankle systolic pressure divided by brachial systolic pressure. Normal is 1.0 to 1.4, and 0.4 to 0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease, so 0.6 is moderate disease. Exertional calf pain relieved by rest with cool feet and faint pulses fits arterial claudication, whereas venous disease causes heaviness with swelling and is relieved by elevation. Calcified vessels raise the index above 1.4, so a low value is not explained by calcification.

question: A 44-year-old man with neck pain has weakness of shoulder abduction, a diminished biceps reflex, and numbness over the lateral upper arm. MRI shows a herniation at C4 to C5 that compresses the exiting root at that level in the foramen. Which nerve root explains the deficit?

options.A: The C6 root, which exits at C5 to C6 and supplies wrist extensors and thumb skin
options.B: The C7 root, which exits at C6 to C7 and supplies the triceps and middle finger
options.C: The C5 root, which exits below C4 and supplies the deltoid and lateral arm skin
options.D: The C4 root, which exits at C3 to C4 and supplies trapezius and the phrenic nerve

explanation: The correct answer is C (The C5 root, which exits below C4 and supplies the deltoid and lateral arm skin): In the cervical spine the C5 root exits through the C4 to C5 foramen, because root numbers are named for the vertebra below the exit level, and it supplies the deltoid and biceps with lateral arm sensation. The C4 root exits at C3 to C4. A foraminal herniation compresses the root exiting at that disc level, so C6 and C7 would require lower herniations.

question: A 41-year-old woman has episodic pounding headaches, sweating and palpitations lasting about 20 minutes. Her blood pressure reaches 220/120 mmHg during spells and 128/80 mmHg between them. Urinary metanephrines are elevated and CT shows a 4 cm adrenal mass. Which cell type is the source of the catecholamines causing her spells?

options.A: Zona reticularis cells of the adrenal cortex, which secrete androgens such as DHEA sulfate
options.B: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, derived from neural crest and stimulated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers
options.C: Zona glomerulosa cells of the adrenal cortex, which secrete aldosterone under angiotensin II control
options.D: Zona fasciculata cells of the adrenal cortex, which secrete cortisol under ACTH stimulation

explanation: The correct answer is B (Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, derived from neural crest and stimulated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers): Epinephrine and norepinephrine are made by chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, which are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons. A pheochromocytoma is a tumor of these cells, producing episodic hypertension with elevated metanephrines. All three cortical zones make steroids, not catecholamines, so none of those tumors would raise metanephrines.

question: A 30-year-old office worker has had bilateral posterior neck aching for eight weeks, worse near the end of the workday. There was no trauma, fever, weight loss, cancer history or arm symptoms. Neurologic examination is normal, and end range motion is mildly painful. Which imaging decision is best at this visit?

options.A: Order MRI of the cervical spine to exclude disc herniation before starting manual therapy
options.B: Order a three view cervical series to establish a baseline before any treatment begins
options.C: Obtain flexion and extension views to screen for occult ligamentous instability
options.D: Defer radiographs and begin conservative care, reserving imaging for failure to improve or new red flags

explanation: The correct answer is D (Defer radiographs and begin conservative care, reserving imaging for failure to improve or new red flags): Nonspecific chronic neck pain in a young adult with a normal neurologic examination and no red flags does not meet accepted criteria for imaging. Routine films add radiation and rarely change management, because degenerative findings are common in asymptomatic people. Imaging is reserved for trauma, neurologic deficit, suspected infection or malignancy, or failure of a trial of care. Stress views and MRI are likewise unjustified without specific indications.

question: A 46-year-old man who injected drugs in his twenties has fatigue and years of mildly elevated ALT. Examination shows spider angiomata and palmar erythema. He has never been vaccinated against hepatitis. Serology identifies the virus responsible, which becomes chronic in about 80 percent of infected people and carries a risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Which virus is most likely?

options.A: Hepatitis A virus, a fecal-oral picornavirus that causes chronic carriage in most adults
options.B: Hepatitis B virus, a DNA virus that becomes chronic in most infected adults
options.C: Hepatitis E virus, a fecal-oral virus that commonly causes chronic infection in healthy adults
options.D: Hepatitis C virus, an RNA flavivirus that usually progresses to chronic infection

explanation: The correct answer is D (Hepatitis C virus, an RNA flavivirus that usually progresses to chronic infection): Hepatitis C is spread by blood exposure such as injection drug use and becomes chronic in roughly 80 percent of infections, leading to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma over decades. The chronicity rate is the detail that separates it from hepatitis B, which clears in more than 95 percent of infected adults even though it is also blood-borne. Hepatitis A is acute and self-limited and never becomes chronic. Hepatitis E is also self-limited except in rare immunosuppressed hosts.

question: In a technique course, students compare named adjusting systems. The professor asks which feature most specifically defines the diversified technique, as distinct from instrument and drop table methods, and notes that it needs no special equipment or rigid listing system. Which characteristic defines diversified technique?

options.A: A table with a caudal section that drops away at the moment the thrust is delivered
options.B: Treatment based on blocks placed under the pelvis to change sacral position gradually
options.C: A high velocity, low amplitude thrust to a specific contact using a short lever
options.D: Use of a spring-loaded handheld device that delivers a rapid low force impulse to the segment

explanation: The correct answer is C (A high velocity, low amplitude thrust to a specific contact using a short lever): Diversified technique is defined by a manual high velocity, low amplitude thrust to a specific contact with a short lever. This is the feature that sets it apart from systems built on special tables or devices. Spring-loaded devices belong to instrument methods, the dropping table to Thompson technique, and pelvic blocks to sacro-occipital technique.

question: A 44-year-old landscaper has a deep ache after lifting. Palpation reveals a tender, taut band lying at the most lateral edge of the erector spinae mass, over the angles of the ribs and well lateral to the spinous processes. Which muscle column of the erector spinae is most likely strained?

options.A: The longissimus column, the intermediate division running toward the transverse processes and mastoid
options.B: The multifidus layer, a deep transversospinalis muscle spanning two to four vertebral segments
options.C: The iliocostalis column, the lateral division running from the sacrum and ilium to the ribs
options.D: The spinalis column, the medial division lying alongside the spinous processes of the thoracic spine

explanation: The correct answer is C (The iliocostalis column, the lateral division running from the sacrum and ilium to the ribs): The erector spinae divide from lateral to medial into iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis, and the iliocostalis forms the lateral border over the rib angles. A band at that lateral edge therefore belongs to iliocostalis. Longissimus sits between the two, spinalis hugs the spinous processes, and multifidus is deeper and belongs to a different group.

question: A 60-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has low serum calcium, high phosphate and elevated PTH. Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D level is normal. In which tissue is the active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, produced, and how does this explain her calcium problem?

options.A: Proximal tubule cells of the kidney, through 1-alpha-hydroxylase acting on 25-hydroxyvitamin D
options.B: Hepatocytes of the liver, through 25-hydroxylase acting on cholecalciferol from skin or diet
options.C: Chief cells of the parathyroid gland, through PTH-dependent hydroxylation of circulating calcidiol
options.D: Keratinocytes of the skin, through ultraviolet conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol into cholecalciferol

explanation: The correct answer is A (Proximal tubule cells of the kidney, through 1-alpha-hydroxylase acting on 25-hydroxyvitamin D): Vitamin D is hydroxylated first in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, then in the proximal tubule by 1-alpha-hydroxylase to the active 1,25 form, stimulated by PTH. Failing kidneys cannot make enough active vitamin D, so intestinal calcium absorption falls and PTH rises. The skin makes the precursor, and the parathyroid only releases PTH.

question: A 29-year-old programmer has a restricted, tender right C2-C3 facet joint and reports a right-sided frontal headache with no intracranial pathology on workup. A student asks which neuroanatomic basis best explains why a cervical joint problem is felt in the head. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Cervical sympathetic fibers carry nociceptive signals directly from the facet to the trigeminal ganglion
options.B: Dorsal column fibers decussate at the medulla and synapse on the trigeminal motor nucleus
options.C: The vertebral artery transmits nociceptive signals from the facet capsule to intracranial vessels of the head
options.D: Upper cervical afferents converge with trigeminal afferents on second order neurons in the trigeminocervical nucleus

explanation: The correct answer is D (Upper cervical afferents converge with trigeminal afferents on second order neurons in the trigeminocervical nucleus): Afferents from C1 to C3 descend and synapse with the spinal tract of the trigeminal nerve in the trigeminocervical nucleus. Second order neurons receive both inputs, and the brain misattributes the cervical source to the trigeminal territory. This is convergence referral, which needs no direct sympathetic or vascular relay. Dorsal column fibers carry touch and proprioception, not this relay.

question: A 66-year-old retired miner with advanced COPD has a chronically elevated PaCO2 of 60 mmHg. His arterial pH is 7.36 and he is clinically stable and not in distress. Which finding best represents the expected renal compensation for this chronic respiratory acidosis?

options.A: Increased renal hydrogen ion retention, which lowers serum bicarbonate to about 18 mEq/L as compensation
options.B: Decreased serum bicarbonate caused by increased renal excretion of bicarbonate to offset the retained carbon dioxide
options.C: Increased ventilation driven by peripheral chemoreceptors, lowering PaCO2 toward 40 mmHg within a few hours
options.D: Increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption and generation, raising serum bicarbonate to roughly 30 to 34 mEq/L

explanation: The correct answer is D (Increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption and generation, raising serum bicarbonate to roughly 30 to 34 mEq/L): In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidney excretes more acid as ammonium and reabsorbs and generates bicarbonate, raising it about 3.5 to 4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2. With PaCO2 up by 20 mmHg, bicarbonate rises from 24 to roughly 31 mEq/L or more, restoring pH near normal. The lungs are the diseased organ and cannot lower PaCO2, and a falling bicarbonate would worsen acidosis.

question: A 48-year-old began care for chronic low back pain with an Oswestry Disability Index score of 46 percent. After four weeks of twice-weekly visits the repeat score is 44 percent, and her pain ratings are unchanged. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this repeated measure and change to the plan?

options.A: The score shows recovery of function, so discharge her with a home exercise program
options.B: The score is unreliable after four weeks, so rely on clinician impression until discharge
options.C: The change is below the meaningful threshold, so reassess the diagnosis and modify the plan
options.D: A two point drop confirms steady improvement, so continue the same visit frequency for another month

explanation: The correct answer is C (The change is below the meaningful threshold, so reassess the diagnosis and modify the plan): A change of two points on the Oswestry Disability Index is smaller than the commonly cited minimal clinically important difference of roughly 10 points. With unchanged pain, the patient has not shown a meaningful response after a reasonable trial of care. The plan should be revised by reconsidering the diagnosis, changing interventions, or referring. Continuing unchanged or discharging would ignore what the measure shows.

question: A 52-year-old man with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back develops a bluish discoloration around the umbilicus and a bluish-brown discoloration of the flanks. His lipase is 1,200 U/L. Which process do the periumbilical and flank discolorations most likely indicate?

options.A: Splenic rupture, with left shoulder pain referred from the irritated diaphragm
options.B: Acute cholecystitis, with gallbladder wall edema and obstruction of the cystic duct
options.C: Perforated peptic ulcer, with free air collecting beneath the diaphragm
options.D: Hemorrhagic pancreatitis, with blood tracking from the retroperitoneum into the periumbilical and flank subcutaneous tissue

explanation: The correct answer is D (Hemorrhagic pancreatitis, with blood tracking from the retroperitoneum into the periumbilical and flank subcutaneous tissue): Cullen sign is periumbilical ecchymosis and Grey Turner sign is flank ecchymosis. Together with epigastric pain and a very high lipase, they indicate severe hemorrhagic necrotizing pancreatitis in which blood dissects through tissue planes. Cholecystitis and ulcer perforation do not produce abdominal wall bruising. Splenic rupture causes left upper quadrant pain and Kehr sign, referred pain to the left shoulder.

question: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for four years. She has moon facies, purple abdominal striae and thin skin. She now has acute mid-back pain after lifting a grocery bag. Which skeletal effect of her glucocorticoid exposure best explains this event?

options.A: Disorganized woven bone deposition from osteoclast overactivity, producing sclerotic vertebrae and elevated alkaline phosphatase
options.B: Reduced osteoblast function with increased osteoclast activity, causing osteoporosis and a vertebral compression fracture
options.C: Excess parathyroid hormone from secondary hyperparathyroidism, producing subperiosteal resorption in the phalanges of the hands
options.D: Impaired osteoid mineralization from vitamin D loss, producing osteomalacia with Looser zones in the pelvis

explanation: The correct answer is B (Reduced osteoblast function with increased osteoclast activity, causing osteoporosis and a vertebral compression fracture): Chronic glucocorticoids suppress osteoblast activity, increase osteoclast survival and reduce intestinal calcium absorption, causing osteoporosis, especially in trabecular bone like the vertebrae. A compression fracture after minimal trauma is the typical presentation. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect with normal bone mass, and Paget disease is a focal sclerotic disorder. Hyperparathyroidism is not the mechanism of steroid bone loss.

question: A 42-year-old man has had hemodialysis for eight years and now has back pain and bone aches. His parathyroid hormone is markedly elevated and phosphorus is high. A lateral lumbar radiograph is obtained. Which diagnosis and hormone mechanism best explain the film?

options.A: Renal osteodystrophy, from secondary hyperparathyroidism and impaired activation of vitamin D in chronic kidney disease
options.B: Paget disease, with a picture frame vertebra, cortical thickening, and coarse trabeculae
options.C: Osteopetrosis, from failure of osteoclast resorption, producing a bone within bone and uniformly dense vertebrae
options.D: Hypoparathyroidism, with low calcium and generalized increased bone density without a banded pattern

explanation: The correct answer is A (Renal osteodystrophy, from secondary hyperparathyroidism and impaired activation of vitamin D in chronic kidney disease): Failing kidneys retain phosphate and cannot convert vitamin D to its active form, so calcium falls and parathyroid hormone rises, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism. In the spine the result is the rugger jersey pattern of dense endplates alternating with lucent mid vertebral bodies. Osteopetrosis is uniformly dense with a bone within bone appearance, Paget disease enlarges and thickens one bone with a picture frame margin, and hypoparathyroidism has low parathyroid hormone, which does not fit this stem.

question: A 60-year-old man with diabetes presents with two days of right flank pain, shaking chills and a temperature of 103 degrees F. His pulse is 118, blood pressure is 88/52 mmHg and he is confused about the date. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Refer him to his primary care physician for a urinalysis and culture within several days
options.B: Refer him to his primary care physician for a urinalysis and culture within the next week
options.C: Call emergency services for immediate hospital transport to evaluate for sepsis from a kidney infection
options.D: Advise oral fluids and rest at home, then recheck in two days and compare vital signs

explanation: The correct answer is C (Call emergency services for immediate hospital transport to evaluate for sepsis from a kidney infection): Fever, rigors, flank pain, tachycardia, hypotension and altered mentation in a diabetic patient indicate sepsis, probably from pyelonephritis, which is life threatening. Immediate emergency transport is required, because delay raises mortality. A routine referral, manual care or home rest leaves a patient in shock untreated.

question: A 46-year-old data-entry clerk has night-time numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking the hand. Phalen's test is positive at 40 seconds, the thenar eminence is mildly wasted, and forearm pronation against resistance does not reproduce symptoms. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?

options.A: Pronator syndrome from median nerve entrapment between the heads of the pronator teres in the forearm
options.B: Cervical radiculopathy at C6 from a foraminal narrowing, with a reduced brachioradialis reflex and neck pain
options.C: Carpal tunnel syndrome from median nerve compression beneath the flexor retinaculum, with a possible restricted lunate
options.D: Cubital tunnel syndrome from ulnar nerve compression at the elbow, with ring and little finger numbness

explanation: The correct answer is C (Carpal tunnel syndrome from median nerve compression beneath the flexor retinaculum, with a possible restricted lunate): Night paresthesias in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand, with a positive Phalen test and thenar wasting, point to compression at the carpal tunnel. Pronator syndrome produces forearm pain and symptoms aggravated by resisted pronation, usually without prominent night waking, so the negative pronation test argues against it. Cervical radiculopathy at C6 would bring neck pain and a reduced brachioradialis reflex, and ulnar involvement would affect the ring and little fingers.

question: A 35-year-old warehouse worker develops acute leg pain after repeated lifting with a flexed, rotated trunk. A student asks why the nucleus pulposus most often herniates in one particular direction in the lumbar spine. Which direction is most common, and what anatomic reason explains it?

options.A: Posterolateral, where the annulus is thinnest and the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and weakest
options.B: Superior through the endplate, because the cartilaginous endplate is weaker than the annulus in adults
options.C: Anterior, because flexion pushes the nucleus forward against the thin anterior longitudinal ligament
options.D: Directly posterior in the midline, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thickest in the lumbar spine

explanation: The correct answer is A (Posterolateral, where the annulus is thinnest and the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and weakest): The posterior longitudinal ligament is wide at the vertebral body but narrows opposite the disc, leaving the posterolateral annulus unreinforced and thin. Flexion also squeezes nucleus material backward, so most herniations escape posterolaterally and press on the traversing nerve root. Midline herniation is less common, and vertical herniation through the endplate forms Schmorl nodes.

question: A 44-year-old gardener has had stiff, achy low back muscles for three weeks, with no swelling, no warmth, and no recent trauma. Cold packs have not helped. The doctor considers superficial heat. In which situation is heat preferred over cold?

options.A: When pain is severe, since heat has a stronger analgesic effect than cold at any stage
options.B: After acute inflammation subsides, heat relaxes spasm through increased blood flow
options.C: Over areas with reduced sensation, since heat is better tolerated there and relieves pain faster
options.D: During the first 48 hours after injury, because it speeds the clearance of swelling and bruising

explanation: The correct answer is B (After acute inflammation subsides, heat relaxes spasm through increased blood flow): Superficial heat is preferred for chronic muscle spasm after the acute inflammatory phase because it increases blood flow and tissue extensibility and relaxes muscle. In the first days after injury cold is used to limit swelling. Heat over numb skin risks burns, and it is not superior at every stage.

question: A 28-year-old woman from a mountainous inland village has a diffusely enlarged thyroid, fatigue and cold intolerance. Her TSH is elevated and free T4 is low. Thyroid antibodies are negative, and she eats mostly locally grown foods without iodized salt. What is the most likely cause of her condition?

options.A: Dietary iodine deficiency limiting thyroid hormone synthesis, raising TSH and driving compensatory gland growth
options.B: Excess iodine from seaweed, which transiently blocks hormone release through the Wolff-Chaikoff effect
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue by peroxidase antibodies, typically causing a firm goiter with positive antibodies
options.D: A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which raises both TSH and free T4 and causes hyperthyroid symptoms

explanation: The correct answer is A (Dietary iodine deficiency limiting thyroid hormone synthesis, raising TSH and driving compensatory gland growth): Iodine is required to make T3 and T4, so scarce dietary iodine lowers hormone output, TSH rises, and sustained stimulation enlarges the gland as an endemic goiter. Negative antibodies argue against Hashimoto thyroiditis, and her diet gives no source of iodine excess. A TSH-secreting adenoma would give a high free T4, not the low value seen here.

question: A chiropractor examining a healthy infant palpates the skull and counts on the fontanelles to guide parent education. Because newborn skull sutures remain open for brain growth, parents ask when these soft spots normally become firm. Which pair of closure times is correct for the anterior and posterior fontanelles?

options.A: Anterior at 3 to 5 years and posterior at 6 to 9 months
options.B: Anterior at 9 to 12 months and posterior at 12 to 18 months
options.C: Anterior at 18 to 24 months and posterior at 2 to 3 months
options.D: Anterior at 18 to 24 months and posterior at 9 to 12 months

explanation: The correct answer is C (Anterior at 18 to 24 months and posterior at 2 to 3 months): The smaller posterior fontanelle, at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures, closes at about 2 to 3 months. The larger anterior fontanelle, at the junction of the sagittal and coronal sutures, closes at about 18 to 24 months. Delayed closure can accompany conditions such as hypothyroidism or rickets.

question: A 55 year old man arrives with a day of worsening abdominal pain and vomiting. He lies still and resists any movement. His abdomen is rigid like a board with rebound tenderness, and bowel sounds are absent on a full minute of listening. What is the best interpretation and action?

options.A: Peritonitis from a perforated organ, needing emergency transfer for surgical evaluation
options.B: Gastroenteritis with voluntary guarding, managed with fluids and a bland diet at home for two days
options.C: Renal colic from a stone, managed with hydration and an outpatient urinalysis within the week
options.D: Abdominal wall muscle strain, managed with gentle soft tissue work and a short course of rest

explanation: The correct answer is A (Peritonitis from a perforated organ, needing emergency transfer for surgical evaluation): A board like abdomen with rebound and silent bowel sounds signals peritoneal irritation, and a ruptured viscus is the usual cause. The patient is still because movement worsens the pain, unlike renal colic, where patients writhe. Gastroenteritis gives soft guarding with active sounds, and a strain would not cause rebound. This is a surgical emergency and calls for immediate transfer.

question: A 31-year-old woman is seen four weeks after delivery. For the first week she cried easily and felt overwhelmed, but this resolved on its own. Now she has had persistent low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and guilt about bonding for three weeks. Which statement best distinguishes her condition from the usual baby blues?

options.A: Her symptoms persist beyond two weeks, pointing to postpartum depression that needs evaluation and treatment
options.B: Postpartum depression is diagnosed only when psychotic features appear within the first twenty-four hours after delivery
options.C: Baby blues last about six weeks and peak at one month, so her symptoms are expected
options.D: Her symptoms reflect normal lochia rubra, which commonly produces mood changes lasting until the fourth week

explanation: The correct answer is A (Her symptoms persist beyond two weeks, pointing to postpartum depression that needs evaluation and treatment): Baby blues affect many new mothers, begin within a few days of delivery and resolve within about two weeks. Persistent low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance and guilt beyond two weeks meet the pattern of postpartum depression, which needs screening and treatment. Psychotic features and an early onset describe postpartum psychosis, not depression. Lochia rubra is the red vaginal discharge of the first few days and has no relation to mood.

question: A 10-month-old girl is brought in because her right arm seems painful when lifted. A chest film from an emergency visit shows several posterior rib fractures at different stages of healing, and the caregiver's explanation for the injuries keeps changing. Which imaging should be ordered to evaluate for suspected abuse?

options.A: A single large exposure of the entire infant on one film to limit radiation dose
options.B: A whole body bone scan alone, because it is more sensitive than films for rib injuries
options.C: A full skeletal survey with separate dedicated views of each region, repeated in about two weeks
options.D: Targeted films of the right arm and chest, since those are the complaint sites

explanation: The correct answer is C (A full skeletal survey with separate dedicated views of each region, repeated in about two weeks): Suspected child abuse in an infant calls for a standardized skeletal survey with dedicated views of each body region, and a follow-up survey in one to two weeks finds healing fractures that were initially occult. Bone scan is sensitive for ribs but poor for metaphyseal lesions and is complementary. A babygram lacks detail, and imaging only symptomatic sites misses other injuries.

question: A 45-year-old man's mean arterial pressure rises from 100 to 140 mmHg during exertion, yet his GFR changes very little. Afferent arteriolar resistance rises in response. One mechanism involves stretch of vascular smooth muscle, and another involves NaCl delivery sensed at the macula densa. Which pair of mechanisms maintains this stable GFR?

options.A: Myogenic response and atrial natriuretic peptide release, both dilating the afferent arteriole to lower filtration pressure
options.B: Sympathetic nerve activation and aldosterone secretion, both constricting the afferent arteriole through baroreceptor reflexes
options.C: Renin-angiotensin response and tubuloglomerular feedback, both constricting the efferent arteriole to raise filtration pressure
options.D: Myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback, both constricting the afferent arteriole

explanation: The correct answer is D (Myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback, both constricting the afferent arteriole): Renal autoregulation keeps GFR stable over a mean pressure of about 80 to 180 mmHg. Stretch of afferent arteriolar smooth muscle triggers a myogenic constriction, and increased NaCl at the macula densa signals the afferent arteriole to constrict. Both are intrinsic and occur without nerves or hormones.

question: A 12-year-old boy comes in with puffiness around both eyes this morning and urine the color of cola since yesterday. His mother says he had a sore throat treated as strep about two weeks ago. Blood pressure is above the normal range for his age. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: IgA nephropathy, which causes visible urine blood but usually appears one to two days after infection
options.B: Nephrolithiasis, a kidney stone causing severe colicky flank pain and urine blood with normal blood pressure
options.C: Acute cystitis, a bladder infection with burning, urgency and cloudy urine but no facial swelling
options.D: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, an immune complex kidney injury appearing one to three weeks after a throat infection

explanation: The correct answer is D (Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, an immune complex kidney injury appearing one to three weeks after a throat infection): Cola colored urine, periorbital edema and hypertension form the nephritic picture, and the two week gap after strep fits immune complex deposition in the glomeruli. IgA nephropathy bleeds within a day or two of the infection, so the longer delay here separates the two. A stone would be painful, and cystitis does not cause facial swelling or raised pressure.

question: A chiropractor sets up an anteroposterior lumbar view on a 34-year-old patient and narrows the light field to the area of interest, while 2.5 mm of aluminum equivalent filtration remains in the tube housing. The radiographer asks how these two measures improve the examination. What effect do collimation and filtration have on the film and patient?

options.A: Collimation limits scatter and irradiated tissue, while filtration removes low energy photons, lowering skin dose
options.B: Both lower patient dose by reducing milliamperage, but each reduces image contrast and spatial resolution
options.C: Collimation adds scatter that raises film density, while filtration adds low energy photons for contrast
options.D: Collimation raises kVp automatically, and filtration shortens exposure time to reduce motion unsharpness

explanation: The correct answer is A (Collimation limits scatter and irradiated tissue, while filtration removes low energy photons, lowering skin dose): Collimation shrinks the volume of tissue irradiated, which reduces scatter reaching the film and improves contrast while lowering the dose to the patient. Filtration with aluminum absorbs low energy photons that would be absorbed in the skin without reaching the film. Neither device changes kVp or milliamperage, and both usually improve image quality rather than reduce it.

question: A 65-year-old woman has had left lower quadrant pain for three days with a temperature of 101 degrees F, nausea and no bowel movement in four days. There is focal tenderness with guarding in the left lower abdomen, and the pain does not change with back or hip motion. What is the best diagnosis and plan?

options.A: Constipation from muscle strain; apply lumbar mobilization and advise a stool softener before recheck
options.B: Acute diverticulitis; refer for same day medical evaluation, imaging and antibiotic treatment
options.C: Ureteral stone; encourage fluids and wait for passage before arranging any imaging or medical assessment
options.D: Irritable bowel syndrome; recommend dietary fiber and stress reduction and review in two weeks

explanation: The correct answer is B (Acute diverticulitis; refer for same day medical evaluation, imaging and antibiotic treatment): Focal left lower quadrant pain with fever, guarding and constipation in an older adult is the typical presentation of diverticulitis, which needs same day medical evaluation. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause fever or guarding, and pain unchanged by back and hip movement argues against a spinal source. A stone would produce colicky flank pain, not focal peritoneal signs.

question: A 61-year-old man with a temperature of 102.4 degrees F has had a hot, swollen, painful right knee for two days and cannot bear weight. Aspirated synovial fluid results are in the table. Which fluid pattern is present, and what is the appropriate next step?

options.A: Non-inflammatory osteoarthritic pattern, managed with conservative care, activity changes and joint mobilization
options.B: Inflammatory pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, managed by a routine rheumatology appointment within the next two weeks
options.C: Septic pattern with high neutrophils and low glucose, needing same day emergency referral for drainage
options.D: Inflammatory pattern typical of gout, treated with rest, ice and dietary counselling after crystal analysis

explanation: The correct answer is C (Septic pattern with high neutrophils and low glucose, needing same day emergency referral for drainage): A synovial white count above 50,000 per mm3 with over 90 percent neutrophils, glucose well below serum, a turbid yellow-green appearance and Gram-positive cocci confirm a septic joint. Bacterial infection destroys cartilage within days, so the patient needs same day hospital drainage and intravenous antibiotics, and no manual therapy. Gout would show negatively birefringent crystals, osteoarthritis gives counts under 2,000, and rheumatoid fluid is inflammatory but culture negative.

question: During a neurologic examination, a chiropractic student records the patient's right patellar tendon reflex as 4+ with several beats of ankle clonus on the same side. On the standard 0 to 4+ reflex scale, how should this grade be interpreted?

options.A: An absent reflex with no response even after reinforcement maneuvers are used
options.B: Hyperactive reflex, often with clonus, suggesting an upper motor neuron lesion
options.C: A normal reflex response within the expected range for a healthy adult patient
options.D: A brisk but normal reflex that is common in anxious patients and athletes

explanation: The correct answer is B (Hyperactive reflex, often with clonus, suggesting an upper motor neuron lesion): On the 0 to 4+ scale, 2+ is normal, 0 is absent, 1+ is diminished, 3+ is brisk and 4+ is hyperactive, often with clonus. This grade, with clonus, suggests an upper motor neuron lesion. A brisk normal response is graded 3+ and is not accompanied by sustained clonus.

question: A physical therapist teaching a back school class asks which of four activities loads the lumbar intervertebral disc the most, as measured in the classic Nachemson intradiscal pressure studies of living subjects. Which activity produces the highest pressure at the L3 disc?

options.A: Standing relaxed with weight evenly distributed and the lumbar lordosis kept in a neutral posture
options.B: Walking at a normal pace on level ground with a relaxed arm swing
options.C: Sitting upright in a chair with the lumbar spine supported by a lordotic backrest
options.D: Lifting a weight from the floor with a rounded, flexed lumbar spine and a held load

explanation: The correct answer is D (Lifting a weight from the floor with a rounded, flexed lumbar spine and a held load): Intradiscal pressure is lowest lying supine and rises with standing, sitting, and forward flexion. It is highest when a load is lifted with a flexed spine because the bending moment and the weight act on a long lever. Supported upright sitting and standing are lower, and walking adds little compressive force. Lifting with a rounded spine therefore ranks first.

question: A 45-year-old man who restores antique felt hats using an old workshop formulation reports tremor, irritability, unusual shyness, and bleeding gums. Recently he has become anxious around customers and drools heavily. Which toxin exposure best fits this historic occupational presentation?

options.A: Mercury from felt processing, causing intention tremor, erethism, gingivitis, and neuropsychiatric change
options.B: Cadmium, which causes proximal tubular injury, osteomalacia, and emphysema in battery and smelter workers
options.C: Arsenic, which causes Mees lines, garlic odor on the breath, and a peripheral neuropathy after exposure
options.D: Lead, which causes basophilic stippling, a gingival line, wrist drop, and abdominal colic in workers

explanation: The correct answer is A (Mercury from felt processing, causing intention tremor, erethism, gingivitis, and neuropsychiatric change): Mercury was used to process felt, and chronic exposure causes erethism (shyness, irritability), intention tremor, gingivitis, and excessive salivation, which gave rise to the phrase mad as a hatter. Lead produces colic, wrist drop, and stippled red cells. Arsenic produces Mees lines and garlic breath, and cadmium targets the kidney and bone.

question: A new rapid test for a bone infection correctly returns negative in 190 of 200 healthy volunteers confirmed to be free of the infection. The developer wants the name of this property and its clinical use when the result is positive. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Positive predictive value of ninety-five percent, which does not depend on prevalence in the tested group
options.B: Sensitivity of ninety-five percent, so a negative result helps rule out disease
options.C: Specificity of five percent, which is the false positive proportion among healthy people
options.D: Specificity of ninety-five percent, so a positive result helps rule in disease

explanation: The correct answer is D (Specificity of ninety-five percent, so a positive result helps rule in disease): Specificity is the proportion of people without disease who test negative, here 190 of 200 or 95 percent. A highly specific test rarely gives false positives, so a positive result helps rule in disease. Sensitivity is measured in people with the disease, so these data cannot give it. The false positive rate is 5 percent, not the specificity, and predictive value changes with prevalence.

question: A 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks of pregnancy reports low back pain that worsens with standing and walking. Neurologic examination is normal, she has no bleeding, fever, or urinary symptoms, and her vital signs are normal. Which management plan is most appropriate for this patient?

options.A: Order lumbar radiographs to identify the cause before any treatment is offered during pregnancy
options.B: Treat with modified positioning and technique, and coordinate care with her obstetric provider
options.C: Withhold all manual care until after delivery and recommend bed rest for the remaining pregnancy
options.D: Use the standard prone table setup with high-force thrusts since the pain is mechanical

explanation: The correct answer is B (Treat with modified positioning and technique, and coordinate care with her obstetric provider): Low back pain in the second trimester without red flags is common and appropriate for chiropractic care. Care should be adapted with side-lying or pillow-supported positioning and lower-force technique, and communicated to the obstetric provider. Withholding care or prescribing bed rest is not supported. Radiographs expose the fetus and are not indicated without red flags, and prone positioning with high-force thrusts is unsuitable at 20 weeks.

question: A 63-year-old woman has hand osteoarthritis with morning finger stiffness that limits mobilization and daily grip tasks. Her skin is intact with normal sensation. You consider a paraffin bath before mobilization. What is the best rationale, and which finding would contraindicate its use?

options.A: Deep heat that reaches the joint capsule, contraindicated by an old fracture of a finger
options.B: Mild cooling that reduces synovial swelling, contraindicated by intact skin and normal sensation
options.C: Conductive heat that eases stiffness before mobilization, contraindicated by open wounds or skin infection
options.D: Convective warm air that loosens the tissues, contraindicated by the presence of Heberden nodes

explanation: The correct answer is C (Conductive heat that eases stiffness before mobilization, contraindicated by open wounds or skin infection): A paraffin bath transfers superficial conductive heat that relaxes tissue and eases finger stiffness, making mobilization easier. The wax contacts the skin directly, so open wounds or infection prohibit it, as do impaired sensation or circulation. It does not penetrate deeply, it is not a cold modality, and Heberden nodes do not contraindicate it.

question: A 30-year-old woman has had a dry cough, fatigue, and painful ankles for 3 weeks. Examination shows tender, raised red nodules on both shins. A chest radiograph shows enlarged lymph nodes at both lung hila with clear lung fields. She has no fever or weight loss. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Hodgkin lymphoma with a bulky mediastinal mass and constitutional B symptoms
options.B: Rheumatoid arthritis with interstitial lung disease and subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules
options.C: Sarcoidosis presenting as Lofgren syndrome with non-caseating granulomatous inflammation
options.D: Primary pulmonary tuberculosis with cavitary upper lobe disease and caseating granulomas

explanation: The correct answer is C (Sarcoidosis presenting as Lofgren syndrome with non-caseating granulomatous inflammation): Bilateral hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum, and ankle arthralgia together form Lofgren syndrome, an acute and usually self-limited presentation of sarcoidosis. Tissue shows non-caseating granulomas. Tuberculosis typically causes unilateral adenopathy or cavitation with fever and weight loss, and lymphoma usually brings B symptoms. Rheumatoid nodules are firm subcutaneous lumps over extensor surfaces, not tender red shin lesions.

question: An 8-year-old girl is found to have a 25 degree right thoracic scoliosis on standing radiographs. She is Risser 0, premenarchal and still growing, with no neurological findings and an otherwise normal examination. Her parents ask about management. What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.A: Refer to a pediatric spine specialist for bracing review, with repeat films in four months
options.B: Treat with manipulation alone, since it halts progression of curves this size in growing children
options.C: Observe with repeat radiographs in twelve months, since curves under 30 degrees need only exercise
options.D: Refer for surgical fusion evaluation, since 25 degrees in a skeletally immature child meets the criteria

explanation: The correct answer is A (Refer to a pediatric spine specialist for bracing review, with repeat films in four months): A curve of 25 degrees in a child who is Risser 0 has a high risk of progression, and bracing is generally considered for growing patients with curves from about 25 to 40 degrees. Referral to an orthopedic spine specialist with close radiographic follow-up every few months is appropriate. Twelve-month observation is too long, manipulation has not been shown to stop progression, and fusion is reserved for much larger curves.

question: Across two seated visits a 52-year-old man's office blood pressure readings were averaged after proper cuff placement and rest. Using the adult classification in which stage 2 hypertension begins at 140 over 90 mmHg, which average reading meets stage 2?

options.A: An average of 138 over 88 mmHg across two seated office visits with correct technique
options.B: An average of 128 over 78 mmHg across two seated office visits with correct technique
options.C: An average of 134 over 84 mmHg across two seated office visits with correct technique
options.D: An average of 142 over 86 mmHg across two seated visits

explanation: The correct answer is D (An average of 142 over 86 mmHg across two seated visits): Stage 2 hypertension begins at a systolic pressure of 140 mmHg or a diastolic pressure of 90 mmHg, and the higher category governs. An average of 142 over 86 reaches stage 2 through its systolic value. The readings of 138 over 88 and 134 over 84 fall in stage 1, and 128 over 78 is only elevated.

question: A 24-year-old man has had three weeks of bloody diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain and low back stiffness with sacroiliac joint tenderness. Stool studies and a serum inflammatory marker are in the table. Which conclusion do these results best support, and what should follow?

options.A: Celiac disease, confirmed by the elevated stool calprotectin as a specific marker for gluten enteropathy
options.B: Functional bowel disorder, so reassurance and dietary changes are appropriate while the sacroiliac pain is treated
options.C: Infectious colitis from Salmonella, to be treated empirically with an antibiotic course and repeat stool culture
options.D: Intestinal mucosal inflammation consistent with inflammatory bowel disease, warranting gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy

explanation: The correct answer is D (Intestinal mucosal inflammation consistent with inflammatory bowel disease, warranting gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy): Fecal calprotectin is released by neutrophils in the intestinal lumen, and a level above about 200 mcg/g separates inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome, where it stays under 50. Positive occult blood, a raised CRP, negative cultures and sacroiliac involvement point to Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis with an enteropathic spondyloarthropathy. Endoscopy with biopsy confirms the diagnosis and guides treatment.

question: A radiologist reviewing a chest CT of a 62-year-old man must divide the mediastinum into superior and inferior compartments for the mass report. On the surface of the chest, which palpable landmark lies at the level of the plane that separates the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum?

options.A: Xiphisternal joint, the junction of the sternal body and xiphoid process near the T9 vertebra
options.B: Costal margin, the lower edge of the thoracic cage formed by costal cartilages seven to ten
options.C: Sternal angle, at the manubriosternal joint level with the second costal cartilage
options.D: Jugular notch, the superior border of the manubrium level with the T2 to T3 vertebrae

explanation: The correct answer is C (Sternal angle, at the manubriosternal joint level with the second costal cartilage): The sternal angle is the palpable ridge at the manubriosternal joint and lies in the transverse thoracic plane through the T4 to T5 intervertebral disc. That plane separates the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum and also marks the second costal cartilage and the carina. The jugular notch is higher and the xiphisternal joint and costal margin are far lower.

question: During bladder filling, sympathetic hypogastric fibers relax the detrusor and contract the internal sphincter. A neurology student reviewing continence asks which nerve supplies the voluntary external urethral sphincter that a person contracts to delay voiding after the stretch reflex begins. Which nerve is it?

options.A: Pelvic splanchnic nerves, parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 that contract the detrusor during emptying
options.B: Hypogastric nerve, sympathetic fibers from T10 to L2 providing voluntary external sphincter control
options.C: Pudendal nerve, a somatic nerve from S2 to S4 carrying motor fibers to striated muscle
options.D: Genitofemoral nerve, a somatic branch of L1 and L2 supplying the cremaster and urethral sphincter

explanation: The correct answer is C (Pudendal nerve, a somatic nerve from S2 to S4 carrying motor fibers to striated muscle): The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, supplied by the pudendal nerve from S2 to S4 through Onuf's nucleus. The hypogastric nerve is sympathetic and relaxes the detrusor, while the pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic and drive detrusor contraction for emptying. The genitofemoral nerve has no role in sphincter control.

question: During palpation practice at the base of the neck, a student feels a large midline spinous process that stands out when the head is flexed. It is long, not bifid, and easily felt through the skin. Which vertebra does this description identify?

options.A: C6, the vertebra with a large anterior carotid tubercle but a short bifid spinous process
options.B: T1, the first thoracic vertebra, with a short horizontal spinous process and a full rib facet
options.C: C2, the axis, with a large bifid spinous process that is deep to the skin
options.D: C7, the vertebra prominens, with its long spinous process ending in a single tubercle

explanation: The correct answer is D (C7, the vertebra prominens, with its long spinous process ending in a single tubercle): C7 is the vertebra prominens because its spinous process is long, nonbifid and easy to palpate at the cervicothoracic junction. The axis spinous process is large but bifid and deeply placed. T1 has a full costal facet and a shorter process, and C6 is marked by its carotid tubercle with a bifid process.

question: A 34-year-old woman with heavy menstrual periods reports four months of fatigue and breathlessness climbing stairs. She looks pale. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL and an elevated total iron-binding capacity. Which conclusion and next step best fit this panel?

options.A: Anemia of chronic disease, so the underlying inflammatory condition should be sought before any iron
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia, so the source of chronic blood loss should be identified and treated promptly
options.C: Beta thalassemia trait, so electrophoresis should be ordered because ferritin and binding capacity are normal
options.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency, so intrinsic factor antibodies should be measured and cobalamin started

explanation: The correct answer is B (Iron deficiency anemia, so the source of chronic blood loss should be identified and treated promptly): Low ferritin with a high total iron-binding capacity and microcytosis is the signature of iron deficiency, and in a premenopausal woman with heavy periods the bleeding source is the thing to pursue. Anemia of chronic disease would show normal or high ferritin with a low binding capacity. B12 deficiency produces large cells, not small ones. Thalassemia trait gives small cells but ferritin and iron studies stay normal.

question: A 31-year-old distance runner has right sacroiliac region pain. Standing assessment shows a right iliac crest 6 mm lower than the left, and tape measurement shows an 8 mm anatomic leg length difference. Her coach asks what these findings prove. What can be concluded from this evidence about the cause of her pain?

options.A: The difference establishes a structural short leg and confirms the sacroiliac joint as pain source
options.B: An 8 mm difference is common in asymptomatic people, so a causal role cannot be concluded
options.C: Because the pelvis is unlevel in standing, the right sacroiliac joint must be fixated low
options.D: The inequality proves pelvic unleveling causes the sacroiliac dysfunction, so a heel lift should be prescribed

explanation: The correct answer is B (An 8 mm difference is common in asymptomatic people, so a causal role cannot be concluded): Small leg length differences of about 5 to 10 mm are common in people without pain, so the finding alone cannot show cause. Pelvic height in standing is also a poorly reliable and poorly valid indicator of sacroiliac dysfunction. Provocation tests and the history are needed before attributing her pain to the joint. A lift or fixation call based only on these numbers would go beyond the evidence.

question: A 45-year-old woman with a BMI of 31 and knee pain tells the doctor, 'I want a plan, and I will start next week.' She has no current exercise routine and says she has already cleared her schedule. Which response best matches her stage of change?

options.A: Explore both sides of her ambivalence about changing, since she is not yet convinced
options.B: Explain the health risks of obesity in detail to raise her awareness that a problem exists
options.C: Help her set a specific plan with a start date, and affirm her commitment
options.D: Wait until she has kept the new behavior for six months before offering any planning help

explanation: The correct answer is C (Help her set a specific plan with a start date, and affirm her commitment): A patient who commits to starting soon is in the preparation stage, so the best help is a concrete plan with measurable first steps and a start date. Raising awareness fits precontemplation, and exploring ambivalence fits contemplation. Relapse prevention and waiting belong to maintenance.

question: A biochemistry student calculates the fate of one molecule of palmitate, a saturated fatty acid with sixteen carbons, as it is fully oxidized in liver mitochondria. How many rounds of beta oxidation are required, and how many molecules of acetyl CoA result from the complete breakdown of the chain?

options.A: Fourteen cycles of beta oxidation, yielding sixteen molecules of acetyl CoA, one for each carbon atom
options.B: Seven cycles of beta oxidation, yielding eight molecules of acetyl CoA
options.C: Eight cycles of beta oxidation, yielding eight molecules of acetyl CoA from the whole chain
options.D: Seven cycles of beta oxidation, yielding seven molecules of acetyl CoA and one propionyl CoA

explanation: The correct answer is B (Seven cycles of beta oxidation, yielding eight molecules of acetyl CoA): Each cycle removes a two carbon unit as acetyl CoA from the carboxyl end. A sixteen carbon chain therefore yields 16 / 2 = 8 acetyl CoA. The final cycle splits a four carbon fragment into two acetyl CoA, so the number of cycles is 8 - 1 = 7. Propionyl CoA arises only from odd chain fatty acids.

question: A 70-year-old man reports shortness of breath on exertion that has worsened over several months. He now sleeps propped on three pillows and wakes about 2 hours after falling asleep, gasping and needing to sit upright at an open window. His ankles swell by evening. Which condition do these history items most strongly suggest?

options.A: Left-sided congestive heart failure with pulmonary venous congestion
options.B: Obstructive sleep apnea with repeated upper airway collapse and arousals during sleep
options.C: Gastroesophageal reflux with nocturnal acid aspiration and bronchospasm when lying flat
options.D: Chronic bronchitis with productive cough and fixed airflow obstruction from long-term smoking

explanation: The correct answer is A (Left-sided congestive heart failure with pulmonary venous congestion): Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occur because fluid returns to the central circulation when lying flat, and a failing left ventricle cannot handle it. Exertional dyspnea and evening ankle edema fit the same picture. Bronchitis causes chronic cough with sputum, reflux gives burning symptoms, and sleep apnea causes witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness.

question: A 41-year-old warehouse supervisor with chronic low back pain has mastered abdominal bracing in supine and quadruped positions. She holds a neutral spine through three sets of ten-second isometric holds without pain or compensation, and her lumbar motion is now full and painless. Which progression best advances her stabilization program next?

options.A: Move to passive lumbar traction sessions to unload the segments before adding any further active loading
options.B: Replace bracing work with rapid full-range sit-ups to build global trunk strength first
options.C: Add slow limb reaches and standing loaded patterns, such as cable presses, while keeping the brace
options.D: Repeat the same supine isometric holds for six more weeks until each lasts two minutes

explanation: The correct answer is C (Add slow limb reaches and standing loaded patterns, such as cable presses, while keeping the brace): Stabilization programs progress from isometric control to controlled limb movement and then to functional, loaded patterns performed with the spine held neutral. She has met the criteria for the isometric stage, so adding challenge through bird dog reaches and standing resisted patterns is the logical step. Rapid sit-ups load the discs in flexion before control is trained, extra isometric weeks add little at this point, and passive traction does not build the capacity she needs.

question: A neurophysiology tutor reviews how ADH and oxytocin reach the circulation. Both peptides are synthesized in hypothalamic nuclei, and a patient with a pituitary stalk transection develops transient diabetes insipidus. In which structure is ADH stored and released into the blood?

options.A: Anterior pituitary acidophil cells, reached through the hypophyseal portal veins from hypothalamic releasing neurons
options.B: Median eminence capillary beds, where it is stored in glial cells before release into portal blood
options.C: Posterior pituitary axon terminals, reached by axonal transport from supraoptic and paraventricular neurons
options.D: Supraoptic nucleus cell bodies, where it stays stored until it diffuses into third ventricle fluid

explanation: The correct answer is C (Posterior pituitary axon terminals, reached by axonal transport from supraoptic and paraventricular neurons): ADH and oxytocin are made in magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and travel down axons of the hypothalamohypophyseal tract. They are stored in terminals in the posterior pituitary and released into capillaries on neural signals. The anterior pituitary is controlled by releasing hormones through the portal system and does not store ADH.

question: A 52-year-old man comes in for neck pain. He smoked one pack daily for 30 years and quit 8 years ago. He has no cough, weight loss, or hemoptysis, and his last chest imaging was never done. Which statement best describes his eligibility for lung cancer screening?

options.A: Eligible for yearly chest radiographs, the recommended screening test for this risk group
options.B: Not eligible because he must have quit within five years for low dose CT
options.C: Not eligible because screening covers current smokers only, so yearly chest radiography is advised
options.D: Eligible for yearly low dose CT, since age, pack years, and quit time all qualify

explanation: The correct answer is D (Eligible for yearly low dose CT, since age, pack years, and quit time all qualify): Current screening guidance covers adults aged 50 to 80 with at least a 20 pack year history who smoke now or quit within the past 15 years. He has 30 pack years and quit 8 years ago, so he qualifies for annual low dose CT. Chest radiographs are not an effective screening test.

question: A 44-year-old man reports that his ring and hat no longer fit. His jaw has grown prominent, his hands are broad, and he snores heavily. Fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL, and serum IGF-1 is markedly above the age adjusted reference range. Which condition best explains this picture?

options.A: Growth hormone excess from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma in an adult after growth plate closure
options.B: Cushing syndrome from cortisol excess, causing central obesity, glucose intolerance, facial plethora and purple abdominal striae
options.C: Paget disease of bone, with skull enlargement and a markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase in older adults
options.D: Hypothyroidism from autoimmune thyroiditis, with myxedematous tissue deposition in the face and hands, plus cold intolerance

explanation: The correct answer is A (Growth hormone excess from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma in an adult after growth plate closure): Growth hormone stimulates the liver to make IGF-1, so a high IGF-1 with enlarging hands, jaw and soft tissue points to acromegaly, usually from a pituitary adenoma. Growth hormone also antagonizes insulin, which explains the raised glucose. Hypothyroidism and Cushing syndrome have different laboratory findings and do not enlarge the jaw and hands. Paget disease raises alkaline phosphatase, not IGF-1.

question: A 45-year-old woman has had a sore throat and a foreign body sensation on swallowing for months, with ear pain when she turns her head. She has no fever, and oropharyngeal examination is normal. A lateral cervical radiograph is obtained. Which diagnosis and symptom pattern best fit the film?

options.A: Retropharyngeal abscess, with prevertebral swelling and fever, requiring emergent referral
options.B: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia, with paroxysmal lancinating throat pain triggered by swallowing and normal imaging
options.C: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction, with preauricular pain, clicking, and limited mouth opening
options.D: Eagle syndrome, an elongated styloid process or ossified stylohyoid ligament that irritates nearby nerves and pharynx

explanation: The correct answer is D (Eagle syndrome, an elongated styloid process or ossified stylohyoid ligament that irritates nearby nerves and pharynx): The styloid process longer than about 30 mm, or an ossified stylohyoid ligament, can press on the glossopharyngeal nerve and pharyngeal wall and cause throat pain, dysphagia, and referred ear pain with head turning. The film shows a long styloid extending below the mandibular angle. Abscess needs fever and prevertebral swelling, neuralgia shows normal bone, and temporomandibular dysfunction centers on the jaw.

question: A 48-year-old man has had painless swelling of the right shoulder for six months. He has lost pain and temperature sensation over both arms but retains light touch, and his hands are weak. An AP shoulder film shows humeral head resorption with debris. Which mechanism best explains the joint destruction?

options.A: Avascular necrosis from corticosteroid exposure, producing subchondral collapse of the humeral head
options.B: Septic arthritis from hematogenous seeding, producing rapid cartilage destruction
options.C: Neuropathic arthropathy from loss of pain and protective sensation caused by a cervical syrinx
options.D: Rotator cuff arthropathy from a chronic supraspinatus tear, producing superior humeral migration
