question: A 50 year old woman, two years past menopause, finds a painless lump in the upper outer right breast. It is hard, irregular in outline and does not move when pushed against the chest wall. There is no nipple discharge. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this finding?

options.A: Fibrocystic change is likely, so reexamine after the next cycle and recommend reducing caffeine intake
options.B: Malignancy is suspected, so refer urgently for diagnostic mammography, ultrasound and biopsy
options.C: A fibroadenoma, since it is firm and rubbery, so monitor its size with repeat palpation
options.D: Mastitis is likely, so suggest warm compresses and antibiotic assessment if redness appears next week

explanation: The correct answer is B (Malignancy is suspected, so refer urgently for diagnostic mammography, ultrasound and biopsy): A hard, irregular, fixed, painless mass in a postmenopausal woman has features that suggest cancer, and she needs prompt imaging and biopsy. Fibrocystic change fluctuates with the cycle and is usually tender. Fibroadenomas are mobile and rubbery, and mastitis brings warmth, redness and pain. The chiropractor refers and does not wait to watch the lump.

question: A 70-year-old woman has lost three inches of height and has a worsening thoracic kyphosis without any trauma. She takes no medications and has normal calcium and alkaline phosphatase. A lateral thoracolumbar film shows biconcave vertebrae and thin cortices. Which diagnosis and trabecular pattern are correct?

options.A: Senile osteoporosis, with accentuated vertical trabeculae because horizontal trabeculae resorb first
options.B: Paget disease, with thickened coarse trabeculae and a picture frame vertebra
options.C: Multiple myeloma, in which discrete well defined lytic lesions replace the trabecular pattern
options.D: Osteomalacia, with indistinct blurred trabeculae and Looser zones

explanation: The correct answer is A (Senile osteoporosis, with accentuated vertical trabeculae because horizontal trabeculae resorb first): Senile osteoporosis lowers bone mass, thins the cortices and causes biconcave or wedge vertebral deformity. Non-weight-bearing horizontal trabeculae are lost first, so the remaining vertical trabeculae look prominent. Osteomalacia gives blurred trabeculae, an elevated alkaline phosphatase and Looser zones. Paget disease enlarges the bone, and myeloma produces discrete lytic defects, which are not described here.

question: A 50-year-old fair-skinned landscaper shows you a mole on his upper back that his wife says has grown over six months. It measures 8 mm across, with a notched irregular border and mixed brown, black and red areas. One half does not match the other. Which feature set makes this lesion suspicious for melanoma?

options.A: Symmetry, smooth border, uniform tan color and stable size, describing a benign nevus needing annual observation
options.B: A waxy, stuck-on scaly surface, which characterizes seborrheic keratosis and carries no malignant potential
options.C: A pearly raised border with central ulceration and telangiectasia, characterizing basal cell carcinoma rather than melanoma
options.D: Asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolution, needing urgent dermatology referral

explanation: The correct answer is D (Asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolution, needing urgent dermatology referral): The ABCDE mnemonic stands for asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter greater than 6 mm and evolution. This mole shows all five, so it needs prompt dermatology referral for biopsy. A symmetric, uniform, stable mole is benign. Basal cell carcinoma looks pearly with telangiectasia, and seborrheic keratosis looks waxy and stuck on.

question: A 54-year-old woman has had four urinary tract infections in 18 months and now reports aching right flank discomfort. Her urinalysis is shown in the exhibit. Which type of kidney stone is most likely forming, and what is the underlying cause?

options.A: Uric acid stone, formed because persistently acidic urine and hyperuricemia precipitate urate
options.B: Cystine stone, formed because of inherited defective tubular reabsorption of dibasic amino acids
options.C: Struvite stone, formed because urease-splitting bacteria alkalinize the urine and raise ammonia
options.D: Calcium oxalate stone, formed because hyperoxaluria follows a high dietary intake of spinach

explanation: The correct answer is C (Struvite stone, formed because urease-splitting bacteria alkalinize the urine and raise ammonia): Alkaline urine with nitrite, pyuria, and coffin-lid prism crystals indicates infection with a urease-producing organism such as Proteus. Urease splits urea into ammonia, raising pH and favoring magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals, which form staghorn struvite stones. Uric acid and cystine stones form in acidic urine, and calcium oxalate stones are not driven by infection.

question: A 72-year-old retired teacher has a stooped posture and takes short, rapid, shuffling steps that seem to chase his center of gravity. He hesitates when starting to walk, has reduced arm swing, and turns his whole body as a block. Which gait pattern does he demonstrate?

options.A: Sensory ataxic gait, with foot slapping and heavy reliance on visual guidance to walk
options.B: Parkinsonian festinating gait, with shuffling steps, stooped posture and hesitation on starting
options.C: Cerebellar ataxic gait, with a wide base and irregular, lurching foot placement
options.D: Antalgic gait, with a shortened stance phase on the painful limb and quick weight transfer

explanation: The correct answer is B (Parkinsonian festinating gait, with shuffling steps, stooped posture and hesitation on starting): Short rapid steps, stooping, start hesitation, reduced arm swing and en bloc turning are the features of parkinsonian gait. Festination describes the quickening steps. Cerebellar ataxia is wide based and irregular. Sensory ataxia slaps the feet, and antalgic gait is a painful limp.

question: A 24-year-old man reports six months of dull low back pain and morning stiffness lasting over an hour that improves with exercise and worsens with rest. Pelvic radiographs show blurred, indistinct sacroiliac joint margins on both sides. Which pairing best describes the genetic association and the earliest site of involvement in this condition?

options.A: HLA-B27 positivity, with inflammation beginning at the sacroiliac joints before ascending the spine
options.B: HLA-DR3 positivity, with inflammation beginning at the lumbar facet joints before spreading to the hips
options.C: HLA-DR4 positivity, with erosive inflammation beginning in the small joints of the hands and wrists
options.D: HLA-B27 positivity, with inflammation beginning in the cervical spine before descending to the sacroiliac joints

explanation: The correct answer is A (HLA-B27 positivity, with inflammation beginning at the sacroiliac joints before ascending the spine): Ankylosing spondylitis is strongly linked to HLA-B27 and characteristically starts with sacroiliitis, then ascends through the lumbar, thoracic and cervical spine. Inflammatory back pain with prolonged morning stiffness that eases with activity in a young man fits this pattern. The rheumatoid pairing fails because rheumatoid arthritis targets the hand joints and carries HLA-DR4. The cervical-first pairing fails because the axial disease moves upward from the sacroiliac joints, not downward.

question: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing hand and wrist pain and morning stiffness reports neck pain and brief electric sensations down the spine when she flexes her neck. A lateral cervical radiograph is obtained in flexion. Which diagnosis best explains the findings?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis with transverse ligament laxity causing atlantoaxial subluxation and erosion of the dens
options.B: Os odontoideum with a separate ossicle above a hypoplastic dens and C1 instability
options.C: Ankylosing spondylitis with syndesmophytes and anterior atlantoaxial subluxation
options.D: Type II odontoid fracture from remote trauma with displacement of the dens and C1 arch

explanation: The correct answer is A (Rheumatoid arthritis with transverse ligament laxity causing atlantoaxial subluxation and erosion of the dens): Long-standing inflammatory arthritis of the hands with a widened atlantodental interval and an eroded dens indicates rheumatoid arthritis, in which synovitis weakens the transverse ligament and allows C1 to slide forward in flexion. The lhermitte-type symptoms warn of cord risk. Os odontoideum has a smooth corticated ossicle without erosion, a fracture needs trauma, and ankylosing spondylitis produces fusion rather than erosion.

question: A 56-year-old woman has numbness over the medial leg and medial malleolus after surgeons harvested a long vein from her leg for a coronary bypass graft. The injured nerve travels with the great saphenous vein. Which nerve gives sensation to the medial leg?

options.A: Sural nerve, which supplies skin of the lateral ankle and the lateral border of the foot
options.B: Saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve
options.C: Obturator nerve, which supplies skin of the medial thigh and the adductor muscle group
options.D: Superficial fibular nerve, which supplies skin of the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot

explanation: The correct answer is B (Saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve): The saphenous nerve is a cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve that accompanies the great saphenous vein below the knee and supplies the medial leg and medial malleolus. Vein harvest can bruise or cut it. The sural nerve serves the lateral ankle, the superficial fibular nerve serves the anterolateral leg, and the obturator nerve serves the medial thigh.

question: A 13-year-old girl has a right thoracic rib prominence found at a school screening and reports mild back ache only when she bends forward. On the Adams forward bending test the rib hump remains visible, and her leg lengths are equal. Which finding and next step are best?

options.A: Structural scoliosis, so begin spinal manipulation and defer imaging until progression is documented by clinical measures
options.B: Functional scoliosis from postural habit, so reassure the family and recheck in one year
options.C: Structural scoliosis, so obtain a standing full spine radiograph to measure the Cobb angle
options.D: Functional scoliosis from leg length inequality, so prescribe a heel lift at once

explanation: The correct answer is C (Structural scoliosis, so obtain a standing full spine radiograph to measure the Cobb angle): A functional curve straightens with forward bending, but a rib hump that persists on the Adams test shows vertebral rotation, so the scoliosis is structural. A standing posteroanterior full spine film allows measurement of the Cobb angle and Risser stage to judge progression risk in a growing adolescent. A heel lift is not indicated with equal leg lengths. Deferring imaging is unsafe because the curve may progress during growth.

question: A 54-year-old man with right shoulder pain is tested for deltoid strength. He raises his arm to 90 degrees and holds it there against gravity. When you add moderate downward pressure at the wrist, he resists briefly and then gives way partially. How should this be graded and recorded?

options.A: Grade 5 of 5, full range against gravity and normal strength holding against maximum resistance
options.B: Grade 4 of 5, full range against gravity with some resistance but short of normal strength
options.C: Grade 3 of 5, full range against gravity but unable to tolerate any added examiner resistance
options.D: Grade 2 of 5, movement through range only when gravity is removed by supporting the arm

explanation: The correct answer is B (Grade 4 of 5, full range against gravity with some resistance but short of normal strength): The patient moves against gravity and tolerates some resistance but yields before the examiner's full force, which is the definition of grade 4. Grade 3 would give way to any added resistance, and grade 5 would hold against strong pressure. Grade 2 applies only when gravity must be removed for movement to occur.

question: A student dissects the ligaments lining the anterior wall of the spinal canal. Within the vertebral canal the posterior longitudinal ligament runs down the back of the vertebral bodies. At the level of the axis, which ligament does it become as it continues upward?

options.A: The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane, which spans the front of the atlas and the occiput
options.B: The apical ligament of the dens, which joins the tip of the dens to the basion
options.C: The tectorial membrane, which continues to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum
options.D: The cruciate ligament of the atlas, whose longitudinal band joins the occiput to C2

explanation: The correct answer is C (The tectorial membrane, which continues to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum): At the axis the posterior longitudinal ligament continues upward as the tectorial membrane to the front of the foramen magnum, lying behind the cruciate ligament inside the canal. The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane continues the anterior longitudinal ligament. The apical ligament and cruciate ligament are separate structures around the dens.

question: A 50-year-old man has thirst and paresthesia in both feet. His fasting glucose of 138 mg/dL, random glucose of 214 mg/dL and HbA1c of 7.1 percent are in the table. A student asks which HbA1c threshold supports a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus when confirmed by repeat testing. Which value applies?

options.A: 8.0 percent or higher, the level at which treatment intensification is usually started
options.B: 5.7 percent or higher, which is the lower limit of the prediabetes range
options.C: 7.0 percent or higher, the number used for the fasting glucose cutoff in mmol per liter
options.D: 6.5 percent or higher, confirmed on a second occasion or alongside another abnormal diagnostic test

explanation: The correct answer is D (6.5 percent or higher, confirmed on a second occasion or alongside another abnormal diagnostic test): The American Diabetes Association diagnostic criteria include an HbA1c of 6.5 percent or higher, a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with symptoms. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, a result is confirmed by repeat testing or by a second abnormal test. HbA1c from 5.7 to 6.4 percent is prediabetes, and higher values are used for treatment decisions, not diagnosis.

question: A 44-year-old man has right neck and arm pain with a positive Spurling test. Over three days his triceps strength has fallen from 5 to 3 out of 5, his triceps reflex has diminished, and he now has trouble pushing himself out of a chair. How soon should he be referred, and for what purpose?

options.A: Urgent same-day or next-day referral for imaging and surgical consultation, since the deficit is progressing
options.B: Continue a four to six week trial of conservative care, then reassess if the deficit persists
options.C: Schedule a routine electrodiagnostic study in two to three weeks while continuing manual treatment
options.D: Refer if bladder or bowel dysfunction appears, which is the threshold for neurosurgical referral

explanation: The correct answer is A (Urgent same-day or next-day referral for imaging and surgical consultation, since the deficit is progressing): Progressive motor weakness over days with a reflex change signals an evolving C7 radiculopathy or compression, which needs prompt imaging, usually MRI, and surgical or neurological opinion. Most stable radiculopathy can be managed conservatively for several weeks, but not when strength is declining quickly. Waiting for bladder or bowel changes would miss the window for protecting nerve function.

question: A dermatology student reviews the integument for a 70-year-old homebound patient with reduced bone density who has had almost no sun exposure for years. Which function of the skin is most directly impaired in this patient and likely contributes to the bone changes seen?

options.A: Cutaneous synthesis of cholecalciferol from 7-dehydrocholesterol under ultraviolet B light
options.B: Sensory reception of touch, pressure and temperature through the dermal and epidermal nerve endings
options.C: Thermoregulation through sweating and dilation of the dermal blood vessels in warm environments
options.D: Barrier protection against water loss and microbial entry through the keratinized epidermis

explanation: The correct answer is A (Cutaneous synthesis of cholecalciferol from 7-dehydrocholesterol under ultraviolet B light): Ultraviolet B light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis to cholecalciferol, the precursor of vitamin D. Without sun exposure this synthesis falls, which impairs calcium absorption and bone mineralization. Thermoregulation, barrier protection and sensation are also skin functions but are not what causes reduced bone density.

question: A 22-year-old rugby player has had a previous shoulder dislocation. With the patient supine, the examiner abducts the arm to 90 degrees and slowly externally rotates it. The patient grimaces, says it feels like the shoulder will pop out, and asks the examiner to stop. Pain is minimal. Which condition does this finding indicate?

options.A: Posterior glenohumeral instability, which reproduces apprehension with flexion, adduction, and internal rotation instead
options.B: Anterior glenohumeral instability with a risk of recurrent anterior dislocation
options.C: Subacromial impingement, which reproduces pain with passive forward flexion and internal rotation of the arm
options.D: Superior labral tear, which produces a painful click when the arm is loaded in abduction

explanation: The correct answer is B (Anterior glenohumeral instability with a risk of recurrent anterior dislocation): Abduction with external rotation levers the humeral head forward, so apprehension reproduces the fear of anterior dislocation. Apprehension rather than pain is the key positive finding. Posterior instability is tested with flexion, adduction and internal rotation. Impingement and labral tests rely on pain or clicks rather than apprehension.

question: A 30-year-old woman has tingling along the medial forearm and little finger, worse when she carries a bag or reaches overhead. The radial pulse weakens with arm abduction and external rotation. An anteroposterior film of the lower cervical spine and upper chest is obtained. Which diagnosis and associated syndrome are most likely?

options.A: Cervical rib arising from C7, producing thoracic outlet syndrome with lower trunk and subclavian vessel compression
options.B: Costoclavicular syndrome from a healed clavicle fracture compressing the neurovascular bundle against the first rib
options.C: Cervical disc herniation at C5 to C6, producing radicular pain in the thumb and lateral forearm
options.D: Pancoast tumor of the lung apex, with Horner syndrome and destruction of the upper ribs

explanation: The correct answer is A (Cervical rib arising from C7, producing thoracic outlet syndrome with lower trunk and subclavian vessel compression): The cervical rib is a supernumerary rib arising from the C7 transverse process, and it can angle the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and subclavian artery over the first rib. Medial forearm and little finger symptoms follow the C8 and T1 distribution and worsen with overhead positioning, and the pulse drops with abduction. The C5 to C6 disc would cause lateral forearm and thumb symptoms. The Pancoast tumor destroys bone and causes Horner syndrome, and no clavicle fracture history is given.

question: A radiologist reviewing the chest film of a 36-year-old woman describes the central compartment of the thoracic cavity that lies between the two pleural cavities and contains the heart, great vessels, trachea and esophagus. What is the name of this compartment?

options.A: The pleural cavity, a serous space surrounding each lung within the thorax
options.B: The pulmonary hilum, the region where the bronchi and vessels enter each lung
options.C: The mediastinum, a median partition bounded laterally by the mediastinal pleura
options.D: The pericardial cavity, a serous space surrounding the heart within the fibrous pericardium

explanation: The correct answer is C (The mediastinum, a median partition bounded laterally by the mediastinal pleura): The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thorax between the two pleural cavities, and the heart sits inside it within the pericardial sac. The pericardial cavity is only the thin space around the heart. Each pleural cavity surrounds one lung and lies lateral to the mediastinum. The hilum is the point at which structures enter a single lung.

question: A 58-year-old woman is receiving a cervical examination. During sustained right rotation with extension held for 30 seconds she becomes dizzy, develops nystagmus, and reports nausea. Symptoms resolve within a minute of returning to neutral. Her blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg. What does the finding imply, and what should the examiner do next?

options.A: Possible vertebrobasilar insufficiency; stop cervical manipulation and arrange vascular imaging with medical referral
options.B: Benign positional vertigo of the posterior canal; proceed with manipulation after performing the Epley maneuver
options.C: Cervical muscle spasm causing reflex dizziness; apply heat and continue with the planned adjustment
options.D: Orthostatic hypotension from low blood pressure; have her drink fluids and repeat the same test

explanation: The correct answer is A (Possible vertebrobasilar insufficiency; stop cervical manipulation and arrange vascular imaging with medical referral): Dizziness, nystagmus and nausea provoked by sustained rotation and extension suggest reduced vertebral artery flow. The correct response is to avoid cervical manipulation and send her for vascular imaging and medical evaluation. Her blood pressure is normal, which argues against an orthostatic cause. Benign positional vertigo is provoked by head position relative to gravity, and muscle spasm would not cause nystagmus.

question: A 26-year-old woman has two months of joint pain, a facial rash across the cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds, and sensitivity to sunlight. Serologic and blood results are in the table. Among the abnormal tests, which one is most specific for the disease this picture suggests?

options.A: Antinuclear antibody, because its titer of 1:640 makes it the most specific test for lupus
options.B: Low complement levels, since consumption by immune complexes is found in no other disease
options.C: Antihistone antibody, which is the most specific marker for idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus
options.D: Anti-double stranded DNA antibody, specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and rising with nephritis activity

explanation: The correct answer is D (Anti-double stranded DNA antibody, specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and rising with nephritis activity): The antinuclear antibody is positive in nearly all patients with lupus, so it is a sensitive screen, but it is also positive in many other autoimmune diseases and in healthy people. Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies are far more specific for lupus, and their titers track disease activity, especially lupus nephritis. Antihistone antibodies point toward drug-induced lupus. Low C3 and C4 reflect complement use and appear in other immune complex states.

question: A 72-year-old retired teacher is 2 inches shorter than at age 40 and reports stiffer, less cushioned movements in the low back. Imaging shows narrowed lumbar disc spaces without fractures. Which age-related change in the intervertebral disc best accounts for the loss of height and reduced shock absorption?

options.A: Hypertrophy of the nucleus pulposus, which swells the disc and shifts load onto the annulus
options.B: Increased proteoglycan content in the annulus fibrosus, which raises its elastic recoil under axial load
options.C: Loss of water in the nucleus pulposus, which flattens the disc and reduces compression resistance
options.D: Calcification of the vertebral endplates alone, which thickens each segment and widens the disc space

explanation: The correct answer is C (Loss of water in the nucleus pulposus, which flattens the disc and reduces compression resistance): With aging the nucleus pulposus loses water and proteoglycan, so it can no longer distribute compressive load hydrostatically, and the disc narrows and the annulus bears more stress. Height loss and stiffness follow. A swollen nucleus would increase height. Endplate calcification may occur but does not explain narrowing, and proteoglycan content falls rather than rises.

question: A 30-year-old man fell onto his outstretched hand from a ladder and has severe wrist pain with median nerve paresthesia. A posteroanterior wrist film is obtained, with the carpal arcs measured. Which arc finding and injury does the film demonstrate?

options.A: Disrupted arc of the capitate and hamate, indicating a hamate hook fracture
options.B: Smooth arcs with a lucent line through the scaphoid waist, indicating a nondisplaced scaphoid fracture
options.C: Smooth arcs with a normal scapholunate gap of 2 mm, indicating a simple sprain needing splinting
options.D: Proximal row arcs broken at the lunate, indicating lunate or perilunate dislocation needing urgent referral today

explanation: The correct answer is D (Proximal row arcs broken at the lunate, indicating lunate or perilunate dislocation needing urgent referral today): The three Gilula arcs outline the proximal and distal surfaces of the proximal carpal row and the proximal surfaces of the capitate and hamate. Interruption of the first and second arcs at the lunate, with the lunate overlapping the capitate and a triangular shape, shows lunate or perilunate dislocation. This is an emergency because of median nerve compression and ischemia, so the patient needs prompt orthopedic care.

question: A 7-year-old girl has had five long-bone fractures after minimal trauma. Her sclerae are blue-gray, her hearing is normal, and her father had similar fractures in childhood. Her platelet count and coagulation tests are normal. Which diagnosis and molecular basis best fit her presentation?

options.A: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome from defective lysyl hydroxylase, with hyperextensible skin and joint laxity rather than fractures
options.B: Marfan syndrome from a fibrillin-1 defect, causing arachnodactyly and lens dislocation with a tall habitus
options.C: Scurvy from impaired proline hydroxylation due to vitamin C deficiency, producing gingival bleeding and perifollicular hemorrhages
options.D: Osteogenesis imperfecta from glycine substitutions in the type I collagen helix, weakening bone and sclera

explanation: The correct answer is D (Osteogenesis imperfecta from glycine substitutions in the type I collagen helix, weakening bone and sclera): Recurrent low-trauma fractures, blue sclerae and a dominant family history indicate osteogenesis imperfecta. Most cases arise from glycine substitutions in the Gly-X-Y repeat of type I collagen, which disrupt the triple helix and weaken bone, and thin sclera lets the choroid show through. Ehlers-Danlos, scurvy and Marfan syndrome each involve connective tissue but lack this fracture pattern.

question: A 38-year-old woman with lupus has taken prednisone 40 mg daily for two years. She now has groin pain with weight bearing and limited internal rotation of the hip. Plain radiograph is normal, but MRI shows a subchondral lesion in the femoral head. Why does this complication occur?

options.A: Steroids stimulate osteoclasts to resorb the femoral neck, leaving a pathologic fracture with intact blood supply
options.B: Lupus synovitis erodes cartilage through pannus formation, while the bone beneath stays viable and well perfused
options.C: Steroids raise marrow fat and impair subchondral blood flow, causing ischemic bone death and later collapse
options.D: Steroid induced hypercalcemia deposits calcium in the joint capsule, producing calcific periarthritis with preserved bone perfusion

explanation: The correct answer is C (Steroids raise marrow fat and impair subchondral blood flow, causing ischemic bone death and later collapse): Osteonecrosis, or avascular necrosis, of the femoral head follows steroid use because of marrow fat expansion, fat emboli, and vascular compression that reduce subchondral blood supply. The bone dies, and the weakened subchondral plate eventually collapses. Radiographs are normal early, while MRI is sensitive. Pannus, calcific periarthritis, and direct osteoclast activation do not explain a perfusion defect.

question: A 28-year-old woman has mild neck stiffness after a minor rear-end collision. Neurologic examination is normal and she has no history of neck surgery. A lateral cervical radiograph is obtained before adjusting. Based on the film, what is the most likely diagnosis and why does it matter for adjustment?

options.A: Posterior arch aplasia of the atlas, a variant making posterior C1 contact and extension stress inadvisable
options.B: Posterior ponticle, a bony bridge over the vertebral artery groove that is harmless to adjusting
options.C: Jefferson burst fracture of the atlas, which needs immediate immobilization and CT before any manual care
options.D: Os odontoideum, which produces atlantoaxial instability and calls for flexion and extension studies before adjusting

explanation: The correct answer is A (Posterior arch aplasia of the atlas, a variant making posterior C1 contact and extension stress inadvisable): The missing posterior ring with interruption of the spinolaminar line at C1 in a young adult without trauma fits congenital aplasia of the posterior arch. It is usually asymptomatic, but the atlas is structurally weakened posteriorly, so direct posterior pressure and forceful extension are avoided. The Jefferson fracture shows lateral mass displacement and cortical breaks, not a smooth absent arch. Os odontoideum involves the dens, and a ponticle adds bone rather than removing it.

question: A 50-year-old man with a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes has a hemoglobin A1c of 7.4 percent. He received a red blood cell transfusion 3 weeks ago after a gastrointestinal bleed. What does the test measure, and which limitation applies to this patient's result?

options.A: Fasting glucose on the morning of the draw, unaffected by recent meals or sleep
options.B: Glucose exposure over the previous 24 hours, with accuracy unaffected by anemia or transfusion
options.C: Glucose control over the previous 2 to 3 days, most useful for adjusting insulin doses
options.D: Average glucose over roughly 3 months, but results are unreliable after transfusion, hemolysis, or hemoglobinopathy

explanation: The correct answer is D (Average glucose over roughly 3 months, but results are unreliable after transfusion, hemolysis, or hemoglobinopathy): Hemoglobin A1c reflects the percentage of hemoglobin carrying glucose, which tracks average glucose over the 120-day red cell lifespan, weighted toward recent weeks. Transfusion, hemolysis, recent blood loss, and some hemoglobin variants distort red cell age or composition and make the value unreliable. It is not a daily or fasting measure, and short-term insulin adjustment relies on direct glucose monitoring.

question: In 1895 D.D. Palmer performed the first chiropractic adjustment in Davenport, Iowa, and the school he founded later grew under his son B.J. Palmer. A student asks which agency accredits doctor of chiropractic programs in the United States today. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The National Board of Chiropractic Examiners accredits the programs and also licenses graduates in each state
options.B: The American Chiropractic Association grants program accreditation through state boards after graduates pass national examinations
options.C: The Council on Chiropractic Education accredits chiropractic degree programs under US Department of Education recognition
options.D: The Federation of Chiropractic Licensing Boards accredits colleges and sets the national curriculum for programs

explanation: The correct answer is C (The Council on Chiropractic Education accredits chiropractic degree programs under US Department of Education recognition): The Council on Chiropractic Education is the agency recognized by the US Department of Education to accredit chiropractic degree programs. The National Board of Chiropractic Examiners administers examinations, not accreditation. State boards license, and the federation of licensing boards coordinates them. The American Chiropractic Association is a professional association.

question: A 52-year-old man with a body mass index of 33 has a laboratory report showing a hemoglobin A1c of 6.7 percent. A repeat test two weeks later is 6.6 percent. He feels well and takes no medications. He asks what these results mean for his health. How should you interpret them?

options.A: Inconclusive, since diabetes cannot be diagnosed from hemoglobin A1c without a confirmatory oral glucose tolerance test
options.B: Normal glycemic control, since a hemoglobin A1c below 7.0 percent is the usual healthy reference range
options.C: Both values meet the 6.5 percent threshold, confirming diabetes, so he needs medical co-management
options.D: Prediabetes, since diabetes is not diagnosed until the hemoglobin A1c reaches 8.0 percent on repeat testing

explanation: The correct answer is C (Both values meet the 6.5 percent threshold, confirming diabetes, so he needs medical co-management): A hemoglobin A1c of 6.5 percent or higher, confirmed on a second test, establishes diabetes. Prediabetes is 5.7 to 6.4 percent, and normal is below 5.7 percent. Seven percent is a common treatment goal for diabetic patients, not a normal range. A repeat A1c is itself an accepted confirmation, so no tolerance test is required, and he should be referred for medical management.

question: A radiologist reviews an AP pelvis of an adult after a fall and traces two lines through the acetabular region to judge whether the anterior or posterior column is broken. Which line corresponds to the posterior column, running from the greater sciatic notch downward toward the ischium?

options.A: The iliopectineal line, which follows the pelvic brim to the superior pubic ramus
options.B: The ilioischial line, which follows the quadrilateral plate down to the ischium
options.C: The Shenton line, which arcs along the femoral neck and the superior obturator foramen
options.D: The Hilgenreiner line, which is drawn horizontally through the triradiate cartilages of both hips

explanation: The correct answer is B (The ilioischial line, which follows the quadrilateral plate down to the ischium): The ilioischial line represents the posterior column and the quadrilateral surface of the acetabulum. The iliopectineal line marks the anterior column and runs along the pelvic brim, so a break in it signals an anterior column injury. Shenton and Hilgenreiner lines are hip alignment references and do not define the columns.

question: A 66-year-old man has 3 months of low back and rib pain that worsens with movement and does not ease at night. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL, calcium 12.1 mg/dL, and creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, with a high total protein and low albumin. Which diagnosis fits, and which confirmatory work-up is most appropriate?

options.A: Osteoporosis with vertebral compression fractures; DEXA scan of the spine and hip
options.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism; intact PTH with a sestamibi scan of the neck
options.C: Multiple myeloma; serum protein electrophoresis with bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cell proliferation
options.D: Metastatic prostate cancer; serum PSA with a bone scan showing osteoblastic lesions

explanation: The correct answer is C (Multiple myeloma; serum protein electrophoresis with bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cell proliferation): Bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and a protein gap in an older adult form the CRAB picture of multiple myeloma. Confirmation requires serum or urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and a bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cells. Prostate metastases are typically blastic and rarely cause a protein gap. Hyperparathyroidism and osteoporosis do not explain the anemia and paraprotein.

question: A 68-year-old man has two months of worsening low back pain, fatigue, and recurrent infections. Radiographs show punched-out lytic lesions in the skull and vertebrae. Serum creatinine and calcium are elevated, hemoglobin is low, and the ESR is very high. Which laboratory finding best confirms the suspected diagnosis?

options.A: Elevated prostate specific antigen with osteoblastic vertebral lesions, suggesting metastatic prostate carcinoma to the spine
options.B: Monoclonal M spike on serum electrophoresis, Bence Jones proteins in urine, and clonal marrow plasma cells
options.C: Markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, reflecting osteoblastic activity in a bone forming disease
options.D: Elevated parathyroid hormone with low serum phosphate and subperiosteal resorption of the phalanges

explanation: The correct answer is B (Monoclonal M spike on serum electrophoresis, Bence Jones proteins in urine, and clonal marrow plasma cells): Punched-out lytic bone lesions with anemia, renal impairment, hypercalcemia, infections, and a high ESR point to multiple myeloma. The diagnostic findings are a monoclonal protein spike, Bence Jones proteins from free light chains, and clonal plasma cells above 10 percent in marrow. Paget disease gives high alkaline phosphatase, prostate metastases are blastic, and hyperparathyroidism does not produce an M spike.

question: A 62 year old man treated for lung cancer last year develops severe mid back pain that wakes him at night. Over three days his legs have weakened, he stumbles on stairs, and he has not passed urine since morning. How should you triage him?

options.A: Message his oncologist and keep the appointment already booked for next month to discuss the pain
options.B: Emergency transfer for urgent MRI and oncology or neurosurgical care, with no spinal manipulation
options.C: Lumbar radiographs today and arrange a routine MRI scheduled within the next one to two weeks
options.D: Gentle lumbar mobilization with traction before referral, to relieve pressure on the spinal cord

explanation: The correct answer is B (Emergency transfer for urgent MRI and oncology or neurosurgical care, with no spinal manipulation): Known cancer with night back pain, progressive leg weakness and urinary retention is metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. Neurological function is lost within hours to days, so emergency MRI and treatment are required. Plain films and a routine MRI are too slow, and manipulation or traction could worsen the cord injury.

question: A skeletal muscle fiber has a resting potential near -90 mV, close to its potassium equilibrium potential of about -94 mV. A patient's extracellular potassium doubles from 4 to 8 mEq/L while intracellular concentration is unchanged. Using the Nernst relationship, how will the resting membrane potential change?

options.A: It hyperpolarizes by about 18 mV, because doubled extracellular potassium drives more potassium into the fiber
options.B: It depolarizes by about 61 mV, because doubling concentration shifts potential by the full Nernst constant
options.C: It depolarizes by about 18 mV, because doubled extracellular potassium shifts EK toward zero
options.D: It stays unchanged, because the sodium-potassium pump fixes the resting potential independent of extracellular potassium

explanation: The correct answer is C (It depolarizes by about 18 mV, because doubled extracellular potassium shifts EK toward zero): The Nernst potential for potassium is about 61 times the log of the outside to inside ratio, so doubling the outside concentration changes it by 61 times log 2, roughly 18 mV, toward zero. Resting potential sits near the potassium equilibrium potential because resting permeability to potassium is highest, so it depolarizes by a similar amount. The pump contributes only a few millivolts. A 61 mV shift would require a tenfold change.

question: A 63-year-old woman with known breast cancer and a lytic metastasis at L3 on a recent bone scan has constant night pain unrelieved by position. Her oncologist has cleared her for supportive care. Which approach should the chiropractor avoid at the L3 level?

options.A: A rotary or high-velocity thrust through the lumbar spine that loads the involved vertebral body
options.B: Co-management with her oncologist, with urgent reassessment planned if new neurologic signs appear
options.C: Education on activity modification, including avoiding heavy lifting and long periods of unsupported sitting
options.D: Gentle soft tissue work to the paraspinal muscles well away from the involved level, oncology informed

explanation: The correct answer is A (A rotary or high-velocity thrust through the lumbar spine that loads the involved vertebral body): A lytic metastasis weakens the vertebral body and risks pathologic fracture under load. Forceful thrust or rotation at the involved segment is contraindicated, while distant soft tissue work, activity advice and oncology co-management are appropriate. The constant night pain suggests progressive bone destruction, so the plan must favor protection and prompt reassessment instead of mechanical correction.

question: A 50-year-old woman has a thoracic radiograph taken for a cough, and the radiologist notes an incidental finding at one lower thoracic level. She has no spinal pain, no history of cancer, and a normal bone density scan with a T-score of minus 0.5. Which diagnosis best fits the film?

options.A: Osteoporosis, with vertical trabecular accentuation from loss of horizontal trabeculae and generalized lucency
options.B: Paget disease, with an enlarged body, cortical thickening, and a picture frame pattern
options.C: Metastatic breast carcinoma, with a lytic permeative pattern and cortical destruction
options.D: Vertebral hemangioma, with thickened vertical trabeculae in a corduroy cloth pattern and no cortical break

explanation: The correct answer is D (Vertebral hemangioma, with thickened vertical trabeculae in a corduroy cloth pattern and no cortical break): The hemangioma is the most common benign vertebral tumor and gives coarse vertical trabeculae at a single level, resembling corduroy cloth, with preserved cortex and normal adjacent bone. Osteoporosis causes similar vertical striations but affects multiple levels and the bone density scan here is normal. Paget disease enlarges the body, and metastasis destroys cortex and is lytic.

question: A 30-year-old climber ascends to 4,500 meters, and alveolar PO2 falls in her lungs. Her systemic arterioles dilate in hypoxic tissues, yet her pulmonary arterial pressure rises. Which statement correctly compares the vascular responses to low oxygen in the two circulations?

options.A: Both pulmonary and systemic arterioles constrict with low oxygen, which raises resistance in each bed
options.B: Pulmonary arterioles dilate to widen exchange area, while systemic arterioles constrict to keep central pressure
options.C: Both pulmonary and systemic arterioles dilate with low oxygen, which lowers resistance in each circulation
options.D: Pulmonary arterioles constrict to divert blood from underventilated alveoli, while systemic arterioles dilate to raise supply

explanation: The correct answer is D (Pulmonary arterioles constrict to divert blood from underventilated alveoli, while systemic arterioles dilate to raise supply): Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction matches perfusion to ventilation by redirecting blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli. In systemic tissues, hypoxia and metabolites cause vasodilation to improve oxygen delivery. At high altitude generalized alveolar hypoxia constricts the whole pulmonary bed and raises pulmonary pressure.

question: A 31-year-old patient sits upright while the examiner palpates the base of the neck with two fingers on the most prominent spinous process. The examiner then asks the patient to extend the neck. During extension the process that was most prominent drops forward into the tissue, while the process directly below stays fixed. Which vertebra is the one that moved?

options.A: T2, whose long spinous process rotates anteriorly as the neck is extended
options.B: C7, whose spinous process palpably moves anteriorly with neck extension while T1 remains still
options.C: T1, whose spinous process moves anteriorly with neck extension while C7 remains still
options.D: C6, whose bifid spinous process is the most prominent and slides forward with extension

explanation: The correct answer is B (C7, whose spinous process palpably moves anteriorly with neck extension while T1 remains still): C7, the vertebra prominens, belongs to the mobile cervical spine, so its spinous process glides forward during extension, while T1 is fixed by the first ribs and does not move. The reverse assignment fails because the thoracic segments are splinted by the rib cage. C6 has a short bifid process, and T2 lies below the fixed T1 so it also stays still.

question: A student is writing a six minute SOAP note on a 45 year old man with low back pain and wants to save writing time with short forms. The examiners score only standard medical abbreviations that the board accepts. Which set of abbreviations is acceptable to write in this note?

options.A: CCx for chief complaint exam, OTx for orthopedic test results, and NDx for neurological diagnosis
options.B: Pt-BPs for patient back pain severity, MRx for manipulation response, and FUi for follow up
options.C: LBPa for acute low back pain, PSp for paraspinal spasm, and TXP for treatment plan
options.D: BP for blood pressure, ROM for range of motion and Hx for history

explanation: The correct answer is D (BP for blood pressure, ROM for range of motion and Hx for history): Common short forms such as BP, ROM and Hx are widely understood and appear on the accepted list, so they save time without confusing the reader. The other sets look professional but each code was made up for this note. An examiner cannot score a finding they cannot decode, so invented shorthand can cost marks. Check the official accepted list before test day and use only forms you are sure of.

question: A 14-year-old boy has a painless firm bump above his right knee that has been present for about a year and bothers him when he kneels. He is otherwise well and has no night pain. An AP radiograph of the knee is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Osteochondroma, a cartilage-capped exostosis continuous with the parent bone marrow
options.B: Giant cell tumor with a lytic eccentric lesion reaching the subarticular surface
options.C: Myositis ossificans with peripheral zonal calcification separated from the cortex by a lucent cleft
options.D: Parosteal osteosarcoma with a dense lobulated mass attached to the cortex by a broad base

explanation: The correct answer is A (Osteochondroma, a cartilage-capped exostosis continuous with the parent bone marrow): An osteochondroma is a bony projection from the metaphysis whose cortex and medullary cavity are continuous with those of the host bone, and it grows away from the nearest joint. It is the most common benign bone tumor in adolescents. A parosteal sarcoma lacks marrow continuity, myositis ossificans follows trauma and shows zonal maturation, and a giant cell tumor is a lytic lesion in a skeletally mature epiphysis.

question: A 30-year-old man is struck in the left chest in a motorcycle crash. He is anxious and short of breath, with a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. His trachea is shifted to the right, the left chest is hyperresonant, and breath sounds are absent on that side. What is the most likely diagnosis and action?

options.A: Cardiac tamponade, with muffled heart sounds and a trachea in the midline position
options.B: Massive hemothorax, with dullness to percussion and flat neck veins in shock
options.C: Simple pneumothorax, observed with a repeat chest film in six hours at the clinic
options.D: Tension pneumothorax, an emergency needing immediate decompression and emergency services

explanation: The correct answer is D (Tension pneumothorax, an emergency needing immediate decompression and emergency services): Trapped air under pressure pushes the mediastinum and trachea away from the injured side, and it produces hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, and hypotension from reduced venous return. A hemothorax is dull to percussion, and tamponade leaves the trachea midline with muffled heart sounds. A simple pneumothorax lacks shock, so this unstable patient needs immediate decompression through emergency services.

question: A 68-year-old man with suspected peripheral arterial disease lies supine for a vascular exam. The examiner wants to palpate the femoral pulse just below the inguinal ligament using only bony landmarks on the anterior pelvis. Which location correctly identifies where the femoral pulse is felt?

options.A: One third from the pubic symphysis toward the iliac spine, over the femoral nerve
options.B: Two fingerbreadths lateral to the iliac spine, over the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
options.C: Midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, over the deep inguinal ring
options.D: Midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament

explanation: The correct answer is D (Midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament): The femoral artery passes under the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The midpoint of the ligament itself, between the spine and pubic tubercle, marks the deep inguinal ring and lies more laterally. The femoral nerve is lateral to the artery, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is far more lateral still.

question: A 34-year-old woman with a healed right femoral shaft fracture lies supine with her hips and knees flexed and her heels together on the table. Viewed from the side, her right knee sits clearly lower than the left, while both knees project equally far forward. What does this Allis test finding indicate?

options.A: Functional apparent shortening from pelvic obliquity, with true bone lengths equal bilaterally
options.B: Shortening of the right femoral segment, producing a lower knee height on that side
options.C: Shortening of the right tibia, with the right knee projecting farther forward than the left
options.D: Shortening confined to the right foot and calcaneus, which lowers the heel contact point

explanation: The correct answer is B (Shortening of the right femoral segment, producing a lower knee height on that side): With the hips and knees flexed and the heels together, the femoral lengths set the height of the knee tops. A lower knee on one side therefore points to a short femur, here from the old fracture. A tibial shortening would instead make one knee project less far forward. Pelvic obliquity changes apparent length and would not be shown by this position of the knees.

question: A 55-year-old man has a brainstem stroke and loses the usual automatic rhythm of breathing while he remains able to hold his breath voluntarily. Experimental work shows that vagal afferent signals from stretch receptors in the lungs terminate inspiration. Which brainstem group generates the basic inspiratory rhythm?

options.A: The dorsal respiratory group in the medulla near the nucleus tractus solitarius
options.B: The pneumotaxic center in the upper pons, which limits the duration of inspiration
options.C: The apneustic center in the lower pons, which prolongs the inspiratory ramp signal
options.D: The motor cortex, which controls breathing voluntarily during speaking and breath holding

explanation: The correct answer is A (The dorsal respiratory group in the medulla near the nucleus tractus solitarius): The dorsal respiratory group in the medulla receives afferents from the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves and sets the basic inspiratory ramp. Pontine groups modulate it, with the pneumotaxic center limiting inspiration and the apneustic center promoting longer inspiration. Voluntary control from the cortex can override the rhythm briefly, but it is not the generator, and the Hering-Breuer reflex only terminates inspiration at large volumes.

question: A massage therapist palpates the paraspinal muscles of a 42-year-old man and explains that the deep back layer holds several short muscle groups lying beneath the large superficial columns. Which group lies deepest, spanning from transverse processes upward to the spinous processes of higher vertebrae?

options.A: The spinalis group, forming the medial column of the erector spinae
options.B: The transversospinalis group, including semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores
options.C: The iliocostalis group, forming the lateral column of the erector spinae
options.D: The longissimus group, forming the intermediate column of the erector spinae

explanation: The correct answer is B (The transversospinalis group, including semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores): The transversospinalis group, made of semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores, lies deep to the erector spinae and runs obliquely upward from transverse to spinous processes. The erector spinae form the intermediate layer with iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns. The segmental muscles are deeper still but the transversospinalis is the deepest of the major groups.

question: A 25-year-old woman woke this morning with drooping of the entire right side of her face, including the forehead. She has had aching behind the right ear since yesterday, cannot close the right eye, and has no limb weakness or speech difficulty. What is the most likely diagnosis and plan?

options.A: Herpes zoster oticus with ear vesicles, which requires urgent antiviral therapy and ophthalmology evaluation
options.B: Ischemic stroke of the left motor cortex, which requires immediate emergency transport for brain imaging
options.C: Trigeminal neuralgia, because unilateral facial pain involves the fifth cranial nerve and weakens the chewing muscles
options.D: Bell palsy from facial nerve dysfunction; protect the eye and co-manage with a physician for treatment

explanation: The correct answer is D (Bell palsy from facial nerve dysfunction; protect the eye and co-manage with a physician for treatment): Weakness of the whole half of the face, forehead included, with ear pain and no limb or speech deficit indicates a peripheral facial nerve lesion, most often Bell palsy. A central stroke spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical input. Zoster oticus needs visible vesicles, and trigeminal neuralgia causes brief stabbing pain, not facial paralysis. The eye needs lubrication and taping, and a physician decides on corticosteroids.

question: A 45-year-old man has had back and left leg pain for two weeks. Over three days he now reports foot slap when walking, 2 of 5 left ankle dorsiflexion strength, and numbness over the dorsum of the foot. MRI shows a large L4-L5 extruded disc. What is the best next step?

options.A: Switch to side posture rolls with greater thrust, since stronger correction should relieve the root
options.B: Continue flexion-distraction three times weekly for a month because extrusions often retract on their own
options.C: Add home traction and re-examine in six weeks to see whether the foot drop improves
options.D: Stop manipulation and refer for spinal surgery consultation because the motor deficit is progressing

explanation: The correct answer is D (Stop manipulation and refer for spinal surgery consultation because the motor deficit is progressing): Progressive weakness with foot drop from a large extruded disc is a surgical indication, because prolonged compression can leave permanent motor loss. Continued manipulation or traction delays the consultation. Greater thrust force risks worsening the herniation. A rapid referral for decompression evaluation is the correct step.

question: A 44-year-old seamstress describes nighttime tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers. Examination shows flattening of the thenar eminence and an inability to touch the thumb tip to the little fingertip. Which nerve is compressed, and what does the motor loss represent?

options.A: Median nerve; loss of thumb opposition from a wasted opponens pollicis muscle in the thenar group
options.B: Ulnar nerve; loss of finger abduction from wasted dorsal interossei muscles
options.C: Ulnar nerve; loss of thumb adduction from a wasted adductor pollicis muscle
options.D: Radial nerve; loss of wrist extension from wasted extensor carpi radialis longus

explanation: The correct answer is A (Median nerve; loss of thumb opposition from a wasted opponens pollicis muscle in the thenar group): Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel causes sensory loss over the lateral three and a half digits and thenar wasting. The opponens pollicis allows the thumb to touch the little finger, so it is the key motor loss. Ulnar lesions weaken finger abduction and thumb adduction. Radial nerve lesions cause wrist drop and spare the hand intrinsic muscles.

question: A 68-year-old woman with controlled type 2 diabetes has six months of bilateral thigh and calf heaviness after walking two blocks. Sitting or leaning on a cart relieves it within minutes, and she cycles thirty minutes without symptoms. Pedal pulses are normal and straight leg raise is negative. Which two impressions best fit this chart? (Select 2)

options.A: Lumbar central canal stenosis producing neurogenic claudication that eases with spinal flexion
options.B: Peripheral arterial disease with vascular claudication from diabetic atherosclerosis of the iliac and femoral vessels
options.C: Degenerative anterior slip of L4 contributing to narrowing of the central canal
options.D: Lumbar disc herniation with unilateral L5 radiculopathy and sciatic nerve root tension signs
options.E: Diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy causing exertional leg heaviness in a stocking distribution

explanation: The correct answers are A and C: Relief with sitting or leaning forward and pain free cycling point to the spinal canal, which widens in flexion and narrows in extension. The grade 1 slip of L4 with facet hypertrophy explains the canal narrowing. Normal pulses and an ankle brachial index above 1.0 argue against arterial claudication despite the diabetes. A single root herniation would not cause bilateral posture related symptoms, and neuropathy would not ease within minutes of sitting.
case_text:
Patient: F, 68 y, 64 in, 172 lb
Vitals: Pulse 76, resp 16, BP 142/84 mmHg, temp 98.4 F
Chief complaint and history: Six months of bilateral thigh and calf cramping and heaviness after walking about two blocks. Symptoms ease within minutes of sitting or leaning on a shopping cart. She cycles 30 minutes without symptoms. Mild low back ache, no bowel or bladder change, no weight loss. Type 2 diabetes on metformin, former smoker.
Examination: Slightly stooped gait without foot drop. Standing lumbar extension for 30 seconds reproduces buttock and thigh heaviness. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 2+ bilaterally, skin warm with normal hair growth, capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Orthopedic and neurological tests: Straight leg raise and femoral nerve stretch negative bilaterally. Patellar reflexes 2+, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Strength 5/5 except great toe extension 4+/5 on both sides. Pinprick intact. Romberg negative. Babinski flexor.
Laboratory and imaging: Ankle brachial index 1.05 right and 1.08 left. HbA1c 6.9 percent, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Lumbar films: multilevel disc narrowing and facet hypertrophy at L3 to L5 with a grade 1 anterior slip of L4 on L5.

question: A 68-year-old woman has bilateral leg heaviness after two blocks of walking that eases when she leans forward. She has type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c of 6.9 percent and a former smoking history. Her reflexes are symmetric and her straight leg raise is negative. Which two examination findings most directly support stenosis rather than arterial disease? (Select 2)

options.A: Thirty seconds of standing lumbar extension reproducing buttock and thigh heaviness
options.B: A recent HbA1c of 6.9 percent with a former tobacco smoking history
options.C: Achilles reflexes graded 1+ on both sides at the time of the visit
options.D: Normal dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses with an ankle brachial index above 1.0
options.E: A negative straight leg raise with a negative femoral nerve stretch test bilaterally

explanation: The correct answers are A and D: Extension narrows the canal and the lateral recesses, so a provocation test that reproduces heaviness in standing extension fits neurogenic claudication. Normal pulses and an ankle brachial index of 1.05 and 1.08 make a flow limiting arterial cause unlikely. Negative nerve tension tests only argue against a single root lesion, and a 1+ Achilles reflex is common with age. The diabetes and smoking history raise vascular suspicion, so they do not support stenosis.

question: A 68-year-old woman with lumbar stenosis symptoms walks two blocks before bilateral leg heaviness forces her to rest. Strength is stable, bladder and bowel function are normal, and she has no progressive deficit. She wants to keep walking for exercise. Which two steps are the best initial management? (Select 2)

options.A: Lumbar extension mobilization with high velocity thrust at L4 to L5 to widen the canal
options.B: Immediate referral to vascular surgery for angiography based on the leg symptoms
options.C: Flexion distraction with a home flexion based exercise program including stationary cycling
options.D: Education on red flags with MRI and surgical referral if deficits progress or function declines
options.E: Two weeks of bed rest with a rigid lumbar support worn throughout the day

explanation: The correct answers are C and D: Flexion opens the central canal and foramina, so flexion distraction and flexion based exercise such as cycling suit conservative care. Red flag education and referral criteria are appropriate because progressive weakness or sphincter change would justify MRI and surgical consultation. Extension thrusts narrow the canal, and angiography is not indicated with a normal ankle brachial index. Prolonged bed rest weakens the patient and adds no benefit.

question: A 26-year-old graphic designer felt a pop in her low back while lifting a box three days ago. She has localized mechanical pain, no leg symptoms, a normal neurologic examination, no red flags, and no prior back pain. She asks how long recovery will take. Which prognosis and reasoning should be documented?

options.A: Fair, because mechanical pain after lifting often becomes chronic and needs many months of scheduled care
options.B: Poor, because a sudden onset of pain predicts lasting disability whatever her age or examination
options.C: Guarded, because the pop she felt suggests a structural injury requiring advanced imaging before care begins
options.D: Excellent, given her young age, first episode, short duration, and no complicating factors

explanation: The correct answer is D (Excellent, given her young age, first episode, short duration, and no complicating factors): Prognosis predicts the course and outcome and is built from patient factors. A young patient with a first episode, short duration, no neurologic deficit, and no complicating factors has the most favorable outlook. Most acute mechanical low back pain of this type improves substantially within weeks. A pop in the history is common with lumbar strain and does not by itself mean a poor outlook or a need for imaging.

question: A 55-year-old accountant has neck pain worse with extension and rotation to the right, plus right arm pain that eases when she rests her hand on top of her head. Spurling test is positive and reflexes are normal. Radiographs show uncovertebral osteophytes at C5 to C6. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Midline disc herniation compressing the cord and producing bilateral long tract signs
options.B: Entrapment of the median nerve beneath the transverse carpal ligament at the wrist
options.C: Narrowing of the intervertebral foramen by uncovertebral osteophytes compressing the exiting nerve root
options.D: Compression of the subclavian artery and brachial plexus between the anterior and middle scalene muscles

explanation: The correct answer is C (Narrowing of the intervertebral foramen by uncovertebral osteophytes compressing the exiting nerve root): Arm pain relieved by shoulder abduction, the Bakody sign, together with a positive Spurling test points to cervical radiculopathy. Uncovertebral joint osteophytes project into the intervertebral foramen and narrow it, especially in extension and ipsilateral rotation. Thoracic outlet syndrome, carpal tunnel syndrome and cord compression produce different distributions and findings.

question: A 36-year-old man is struck behind the knee and later has weak toe flexion, loss of plantar flexion, and numbness over the sole. The deep posterior leg compartment holds tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus. Which nerve supplies the posterior compartment?

options.A: Common fibular nerve, which winds around the neck of the fibula before dividing
options.B: Deep fibular nerve, which runs with the anterior tibial artery between extensor muscles
options.C: Saphenous nerve, a sensory branch of the femoral nerve that accompanies the great saphenous vein
options.D: Tibial nerve, the larger terminal division of the sciatic nerve in the popliteal fossa

explanation: The correct answer is D (Tibial nerve, the larger terminal division of the sciatic nerve in the popliteal fossa): The tibial nerve descends through the popliteal fossa and posterior leg and supplies all the posterior compartment muscles, so injury weakens plantar flexion, toe flexion, and sole sensation. The common fibular and deep fibular nerves serve the lateral and anterior compartments. The saphenous nerve is sensory only, so it cannot explain the motor loss.

question: A chiropractor reads one randomized trial showing benefit of mechanical traction for sciatica, and her own clinical experience agrees with it. She starts traction on a new patient without asking his preferences, and he later says he fears machines that stretch his spine. Which element of evidence based practice was missing from her decision?

options.A: Best research evidence, because a single trial cannot support a treatment decision for sciatica
options.B: Clinical expertise, because the decision rested on the published trial instead of the practitioner's own judgment
options.C: Cost effectiveness analysis, because the fee for traction was not compared with other care options
options.D: Patient values and preferences, which she did not elicit before choosing the intervention

explanation: The correct answer is D (Patient values and preferences, which she did not elicit before choosing the intervention): Evidence based practice integrates best research evidence, clinical expertise and patient values. She had a trial and her own experience, but she never asked what the patient wanted, and his fear of traction matters to adherence and shared decision making. The evidence base may be thin but it was used. Cost analysis is not a formal element of the triad.

question: A 4-month-old boy has persistent oral thrush, chronic diarrhea and pneumonia from Pneumocystis jirovecii. His lymphocyte count is very low, and flow cytometry shows absent T cells and B cells. Deoxyadenosine and dATP are elevated in his blood. Which diagnosis is most likely in this infant?

options.A: Bruton agammaglobulinemia from BTK mutation, sparing T cells and causing bacterial infections after maternal antibodies wane
options.B: Severe combined immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase deficiency, where toxic purine metabolites accumulate and destroy developing lymphocytes
options.C: DiGeorge syndrome from 22q11 deletion, causing hypocalcemia, cardiac defects and thymic hypoplasia affecting mainly T cells
options.D: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome from HGPRT deficiency, causing hyperuricemia, dystonia and self-injury but no profound lymphopenia in infancy

explanation: The correct answer is B (Severe combined immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase deficiency, where toxic purine metabolites accumulate and destroy developing lymphocytes): Adenosine deaminase deficiency blocks purine degradation, so deoxyadenosine and dATP build up and are toxic to lymphocytes, which depletes both T and B cells. This explains opportunistic infection in the first months of life with a very low lymphocyte count. Bruton disease spares T cells, and DiGeorge syndrome spares B cells and brings hypocalcemia and heart defects.

question: A 3-year-old boy with bowed legs, widened wrists and beading along the costochondral junctions is found to have severe vitamin D deficiency. His mother asks how this differs from the same deficiency in an adult. Which statement correctly distinguishes the childhood form from the adult form?

options.A: Childhood deficiency leaves osteoid unmineralized in cortical bone, while adult deficiency impairs growth plate chondrocyte proliferation
options.B: Childhood deficiency disrupts growth plate mineralization, while adults develop unmineralized osteoid in a closed skeleton
options.C: Both forms widen the growth plate, because adult physes remain open and vulnerable to deficiency
options.D: Childhood deficiency reduces collagen synthesis, whereas adult deficiency impairs osteoclast resorption of existing bone

explanation: The correct answer is B (Childhood deficiency disrupts growth plate mineralization, while adults develop unmineralized osteoid in a closed skeleton): Rickets occurs in children and affects the growth plate, where cartilage matrix fails to calcify, producing widened physes, bowing and rachitic rosary. In adults the physes are closed, so the same deficiency causes osteomalacia, with excess uncalcified osteoid and pseudofractures. Both are defects of mineralization rather than collagen synthesis. Adults cannot show growth plate widening because their physes have fused.

question: A 26-year-old man has sharp central chest pain for 2 days that worsens when lying flat or inhaling and eases when he leans forward. Auscultation reveals a scratchy sound in three phases. His ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR segment depression. He had a viral illness last week. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Acute pericarditis, typically viral, with inflammation of the visceral and parietal pericardial layers
options.B: Aortic dissection with tearing pain radiating to the interscapular region
options.C: Pulmonary embolism with pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and right heart strain
options.D: Acute anterior myocardial infarction from occlusion of the left anterior descending artery

explanation: The correct answer is A (Acute pericarditis, typically viral, with inflammation of the visceral and parietal pericardial layers): Positional pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward, a three-component friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression define acute pericarditis, most often viral. Infarction shows regional ST elevation with reciprocal depression. Aortic dissection causes abrupt tearing pain, and pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain with tachycardia and hypoxia but no rub.

question: A 45-year-old woman has had neck pain for 18 months. Light stroking of the posterior neck skin is painful, the painful area has spread beyond the original site, and repeated pressure makes the pain progressively worse. Imaging is unremarkable. Which process best explains her findings?

options.A: Central sensitization with wind up, as dorsal horn neurons lower threshold and enlarge receptive fields
options.B: Peripheral sensitization of nociceptors, because local inflammatory mediators lower the firing threshold at the injury site
options.C: Habituation, in which repeated stimulation decreases the response of dorsal horn neurons over time
options.D: Long term depression of synaptic strength in the dorsal horn, which reduces pain after sustained input

explanation: The correct answer is A (Central sensitization with wind up, as dorsal horn neurons lower threshold and enlarge receptive fields): Allodynia, spreading of pain beyond the injury and increasing response with repeated stimulation are the signs of central sensitization and wind up. Dorsal horn neurons become hyperexcitable and their receptive fields expand. Peripheral sensitization would stay in the injured area. Habituation and long term depression would reduce, not amplify, the response.

question: A 35-year-old woman with thoracic hyperkyphosis is positioned lateral for thoracic spine films. Test images show the lower thoracic vertebrae underexposed while the upper thoracic vertebrae are overpenetrated, because the lower region is thicker. Which technique best equalizes density while blurring lung markings and ribs over the spine?

options.A: Suspended full inspiration with short exposure, and a wedge filter thick end over the lower spine
options.B: Full expiration with high kilovoltage, and a wedge filter thick end over the upper thoracic spine
options.C: Shallow breathing with short exposure, and the cathode toward the upper thoracic region with no filtration
options.D: Shallow breathing with long exposure, plus a wedge filter thick end over the upper thoracic spine

explanation: The correct answer is D (Shallow breathing with long exposure, plus a wedge filter thick end over the upper thoracic spine): A shallow breathing technique with a long, low mA exposure smears the lung markings and ribs across the film while the spine stays sharp. The lower thoracic spine is thicker, so the thin upper region needs extra attenuation from the thick end of a wedge filter placed over it. The cathode should lie toward the thicker lower region because the anode heel effect lowers intensity at the anode end. Placing the filter over the thick region, or skipping filtration, makes the density difference worse.

question: A 27-year-old man presents with fever, a diffuse maculopapular rash, sore throat and swollen cervical nodes beginning two weeks after unprotected sex with a new partner. He is concerned about HIV infection. Which test is best to order first at this stage to detect infection?

options.A: An HIV antibody-only enzyme immunoassay, which is reliably positive within the first two weeks after exposure
options.B: A CD4 lymphocyte count, which is the standard screening test that confirms the diagnosis of infection
options.C: A Western blot alone, which is the recommended first test and turns positive in days
options.D: A fourth-generation HIV antigen and antibody combination assay, which detects the p24 antigen before antibodies develop

explanation: The correct answer is D (A fourth-generation HIV antigen and antibody combination assay, which detects the p24 antigen before antibodies develop): Acute retroviral syndrome causes fever, rash, pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy two to four weeks after exposure, when antibodies may not yet be detectable. A fourth-generation assay detects p24 antigen as well as antibodies and is recommended for initial testing, with an HIV-1 RNA test if results are discordant or suspicion is high. Antibody-only tests can miss early infection, a CD4 count is not diagnostic, and Western blot is no longer a first-line test.

question: A 30-year-old man with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic diarrhea develops wheezing, hypotension and facial swelling minutes into a blood transfusion. He had received two previous transfusions without any reaction. Quantitative immunoglobulin testing shows an undetectable serum IgA level. Which immunodeficiency most likely underlies this reaction?

options.A: X-linked agammaglobulinemia, with absent B cells and low levels of all immunoglobulin classes from infancy
options.B: Selective IgA deficiency, with preformed anti-IgA antibodies reacting against IgA in the donor plasma
options.C: Hyper IgM syndrome, with defective CD40 ligand preventing class switching and elevated serum IgM levels
options.D: Common variable immunodeficiency, with low IgG and IgA and defective plasma cell differentiation in adults

explanation: The correct answer is B (Selective IgA deficiency, with preformed anti-IgA antibodies reacting against IgA in the donor plasma): Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and causes recurrent mucosal infections and giardiasis. Patients can form anti-IgA antibodies, so plasma products containing IgA may trigger anaphylaxis. Washed red cells or IgA-deficient donors are used instead. The other immunodeficiencies lower more classes of immunoglobulin or raise IgM and do not carry this transfusion risk.

question: A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has chronic morning joint pain and stiffness. His rheumatologist manages disease-modifying therapy, and he asks what dietary change might modestly lower inflammation. His diet is currently heavy in processed meats and fried foods. Which recommendation is best supported by evidence?

options.A: Eliminate nightshade vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers, which drive most dietary joint inflammation
options.B: Eat fatty fish such as salmon or sardines about twice weekly for EPA and DHA
options.C: Take a high-dose vitamin A supplement daily to suppress the inflammatory response in the joints
options.D: Replace saturated fat with refined vegetable oils that are rich in omega-6 linoleic acid

explanation: The correct answer is B (Eat fatty fish such as salmon or sardines about twice weekly for EPA and DHA): The long-chain omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA in fatty fish compete with arachidonic acid and yield less inflammatory mediators, giving a modest reduction in joint pain and stiffness. Two servings weekly is a standard target. High-dose vitamin A carries toxicity risk without anti-inflammatory benefit, excess omega-6 oils tilt the balance the wrong way, and nightshade avoidance lacks controlled support.

question: A 58-year-old retired mechanic with chronic low back and leg pain is scheduled for a caudal epidural steroid injection. The physician locates the sacral hiatus by palpating the lower end of the sacrum just above the natal cleft. Which pair of bony landmarks is palpated on either side of the hiatus to guide needle entry?

options.A: The two sacral cornua, remnants of the inferior articular processes of S5
options.B: The ischial tuberosities, which lie lateral to the anal cleft and below the hiatus
options.C: The posterior superior iliac spines, which mark the level of the second sacral foramina
options.D: The tubercles of the median sacral crest, formed by fused spinous processes of S1 to S4
